project.title: Open Problems in AI Evaluation
project.subtitle: A participatory research agenda
project.manuscript: Open Problems in AI Evaluation: Exploring Participatory vs Shadow Research Agendas

rubric.label: Relevance to AI evaluation
rubric.description: How directly the question concerns a claim, practice or decision about AI evaluation.

rubric.label: Research openness
rubric.description: How clearly the available material identifies a remaining research obstacle.

rubric.label: Category fit and granularity
rubric.description: How well the question fits its main category and states a coherent, readable research obstacle at an appropriate length and level of detail.

rubric.label: Stakeholder impact
rubric.description: The importance of the stakeholder decisions that better evaluation could inform.

rubric.label: Research value and grounding
rubric.description: The research value of the question and how credible its available grounding is.

terminology_rules.rationale: 'Capabilities' is an established technical term in AI evaluation distinguishing what a system can do from what it tends to do; replacing it with 'abilities' dilutes precision and overrides human author terminology.
'Propensities' is the intentional technical term in the manuscript for behavioral dispositions under deployment; replacing it with 'tendencies' introduces machine-chosen terminology drift.

terminology_rules.paper_context: Taxonomy Tier 2 (Categories -> Open Problems -> Specific Challenges)
terminology_rules.rationale: Maintain strict 3-layer naming: Tier 1 = Categories (7), Tier 2 = Open Problems (30-50, synced with paper), Tier 3 = Specific Challenges / Questions (100s).
Construct validity captures whether an evaluation actually measures the intended property, distinct from mere statistical accuracy.
'Sociotechnical' denotes coupled human-AI-institutional systems rather than separable social and technical parts.

open_problems.title: Unclear boundaries of evaluated systems
open_problems.description: A model, its tools and the people using it can jointly determine what happens. Evaluators need rules for deciding what belongs to the system a claim covers, and when evidence about one component applies to the whole.

lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Plain-language framing spans models, agents and human–AI workflows. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in T.4 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Define and test claims over explicit system boundaries
Establish when component-level evidence warrants a system-level claim within a specified system boundary

open_problems.title: Unclear definitions of capabilities and propensities
open_problems.description: A test score alone cannot tell us what an AI system can do or what it tends to do in practice. We need definitions that distinguish these properties and can be revised when new evidence about behaviour or its causes disagrees with them.

lineage.what_changed: Merged earlier manuscript items F.2, F.3, F.4 into C.F2a. Thematically related to: F.1, V.1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Accessible wording preserves both abilities and tendencies. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in F.2, F.3, F.4 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Connect ability and tendency definitions to evidence across contexts

open_problems.title: Scores lack a shared meaning across tests
open_problems.description: A higher score may reflect a different test, population or difficulty rather than a more capable system. Evaluators need defensible scales for comparing results and describing how broadly capabilities apply, including when systems exceed existing tests.

lineage.what_changed: Merged earlier manuscript items F.5, F.6 into C.F3a. Thematically related to: F.1, V.2, V.5, T.1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Accessible wording retains both comparability and generality. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in F.5, F.6 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Identify invariant scales and legitimate limits of comparisons
Separate breadth and difficulty from instrument-specific thresholds

open_problems.title: Limits on what evaluation can establish
open_problems.description: Some systems can look identical in every test evaluators can run while behaving differently elsewhere. We need to know which claims can be settled with the observations, interventions and resources available, and what extra evidence would change the answer.

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from F.7 as C.F4a. Thematically related to: F.1, V.3, V.5.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Expresses an assumption-relative limit in accessible terms.

research_targets: Map identifiability limits under stated access and resource conditions

open_problems.title: Weak experimental control and causal diagnosis
open_problems.description: The same outcome can arise from very different mechanisms. Evaluation needs controlled comparisons and interventions that separate model, scaffold, human and environmental contributions. The open problem is to obtain explanations useful for diagnosis while retaining realistic conditions and accounting for interactions between components.

lineage.what_changed: Rephrased earlier manuscript item(s) T.2 into R.T2. Thematically related to: F.6, T.5, V.1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Clear Techniques-level gap spanning black-, grey-, and white-box evidence.

research_targets: Separate causal contributions of models, scaffolds, humans and environments using evaluation interventions
Establish fair and realistic comparisons against feasible human and human–AI workflows

open_problems.title: Unsafe or unfaithful evaluation environments
open_problems.description: A test environment must reveal relevant behaviour while containing harm and protecting participants. Sandboxes, simulated users and human studies can alter the phenomenon they are meant to study. We need environments whose safety constraints, realism and remaining distortions are explicit and experimentally examinable.

lineage.what_changed: Rephrased earlier manuscript item(s) T.8 into R.T5. Thematically related to: T.6b, V.1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Clear general instrument-design obstacle; ecological transfer of the result is a separate validity/deployment question.

research_targets: Determine which environment constraints preserve relevant behaviour while proportionately containing harm
Determine how to protect participants and annotators while maintaining credible behavioural evidence

open_problems.title: Choosing fair and realistic human and human–AI baselines
open_problems.description: What comparison workflow, participant experience, resource budget and prior access make human, AI and hybrid performance meaningfully comparable? The evaluation must distinguish an artificial control from the best feasible alternative available to the people making the decision.

lineage.what_changed: Retained manuscript item T.5 as C.T.BASELINE. Thematically related to: T.6b, F.6.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Separately repairable from causal diagnosis: accurate component attribution can coexist with an unsuitable comparison workflow.

research_targets: Establish fair and realistic comparisons against feasible human and human–AI workflows

open_problems.title: Eliciting consequential behaviour under known conditions
open_problems.description: How can evaluation procedures reveal consequential capabilities, propensities and failures under a specified system configuration and resource budget? We need evidence that the evaluation gave the system a suitable opportunity to act and that the test conditions did not substitute a different capability for the one of interest.

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from F.7, T.7 as C.T.ELICIT. Thematically related to: T.3, F.2, F.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: One primary Techniques problem with clear boundaries and a stated scope; special cases can be nested.

research_targets: Design elicitation methods that separate behaviour revealed from assumptions about resources and opportunities
Identify how testing changes behaviour and bound that distortion in evaluation design
Design and compare tests for discovering meaningful rare failure modes under stated operating conditions

open_problems.title: Discovering rare but consequential failures
open_problems.description: How can evaluators choose scenarios, observation horizons and stress conditions that are informative about rare failure modes in a specified domain of use? Tests need to surface meaningful failures and near misses without confusing discovery coverage with estimates of how frequently the failures occur.

lineage.what_changed: Split earlier manuscript item(s) T.7 to form C.T.RARE. Thematically related to: V.2, V.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Within Techniques, a separable discovery problem; can be nested under general elicitation if space is tight. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in T.7 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Design and compare tests for discovering meaningful rare failure modes under stated operating conditions

open_problems.title: Testing changes the behaviour it is meant to measure
open_problems.description: How can evaluators tell when a system behaves differently because it is being tested, and design comparisons that estimate the resulting distortion? The challenge includes changes caused by the testing protocol itself as well as changes when a system recognises the evaluation context.

lineage.what_changed: Merged earlier manuscript items F.7, T.3 into C.T.REACTIVITY. Thematically related to: T.2, V.1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: A separable Techniques target, although it fits under R.T1 as a focused refinement. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in F.7, T.3 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Identify how testing changes behaviour and bound that distortion in evaluation design

open_problems.title: Developing and maintaining tests in time for emerging capabilities
open_problems.description: How can evaluators prepare, validate and refresh instruments in time to assess emerging capabilities under limited compute and expert time? Adaptive task selection and benchmark repair need to preserve coverage and meaningful discrimination as systems and uses change.

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from T.1 as C.T.TIMELY. Thematically related to: T.4, F.5.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Clear general Techniques question once the capability need is specified; forecasting future needs is separate.

research_targets: Determine how to preserve test coverage, discrimination and verifiability within a fixed budget
Design, validate and maintain tests in time for emerging capability changes

open_problems.title: Scores can support the wrong conclusions
open_problems.description: An evaluation score can reflect shortcuts or features of the test instead of the capability or risk it is meant to measure. Evaluators need to show which conclusions a result supports, for which people or settings, and what evidence rules out other explanations.

lineage.what_changed: Retained manuscript item V.1 as C.V1a. Thematically related to: F.4, T.2, D.1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Accessible wording still spans construct, internal and external validity.

research_targets: Test competing explanations and document evidence for interpretations

open_problems.title: Overconfidence in rankings and risk estimates
open_problems.description: Small or repeatedly selected samples can make model rankings unstable and rare failures hard to estimate. Evaluators need uncertainty estimates that reflect how tests were collected and show which conclusions hold across groups, including where the evidence is too sparse to tell.

lineage.what_changed: Merged earlier manuscript items V.2, T.7 into C.V3a. Thematically related to: V.3, L.2.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Explains two consequences of a common estimation problem. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in V.2, T.7 justifies this restructuring.]

stakeholders: Oversight bodies and people exposed to harms
research_targets: Calibrate uncertainty under dependence, selection and heterogeneity
Design and validate estimates for rare-event rates and uncertainty

open_problems.title: Weak assurance about AI system behaviour
open_problems.description: Passing tests does not establish that a failure is impossible. Formal checks may establish properties of parts of a decision process under stated assumptions. We need ways to assess what tests and proofs jointly establish and what uncertainty remains.

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from V.3 as C.V4a. Thematically related to: T.7, F.7.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Retains the GP while making formal verification one route to evidence.

stakeholders: Deployers, oversight bodies and people exposed to harms
research_targets: Derive bounded assurance accounting for coverage and search limits
Compare formal guarantees with empirical checks of assumptions and scope

open_problems.title: Limited formal assurance for AI decisions
open_problems.description: Formal checks can establish some properties of a specified decision process, but an AI system may include learned components and changing surroundings. Which parts can be checked, how can we test the assumptions, and what conclusions apply to the complete system?

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem C.V6 not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: V.3, F.1, V.5.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: General across learned decision processes, although it can also be a facet of assurance.

research_targets: Compare formal guarantees with empirical checks of assumptions and scope

open_problems.title: Unreliable judges and evaluation methods
open_problems.description: When tests and judges use similar models or data, they can agree while sharing the same errors. We need ways to check difficult answers against trustworthy standards and to test whether whole evaluation methods work, using evidence independent of the systems being evaluated.

lineage.what_changed: Merged earlier manuscript items V.4, V.5 into C.V7. Thematically related to: T.1, V.1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: A defensible compression under independent evaluation evidence; breadth weakens the distinction between grader failure and bad test design. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in V.4, V.5 justifies this restructuring.]

stakeholders: Evaluators and users of evaluation results
research_targets: Develop and calibrate reference standards for hard-to-judge work
Test evaluator reliability with independent evidence and controls

open_problems.title: Weak prediction beyond tested conditions
open_problems.description: Evaluation is useful when it informs behaviour in conditions that were not directly tested. We need models of how results transfer across tasks, users, interfaces and operational settings. These predictions must identify their assumptions and failure conditions rather than treating a benchmark score as a universal deployment forecast.

lineage.what_changed: Retained manuscript item D.1 as R.D1. Thematically related to: D.2.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Clear Deployment home and broad grain.

research_targets: Validate transfer models against held-out operational conditions

open_problems.title: Forecasts break when AI systems change
open_problems.description: Tests of current systems give only partial evidence about later models or systems that learn during use. We need forecasts that state what changes they assume, how far ahead they apply, and how their uncertainty changes when the system evolves in other ways.

lineage.what_changed: Rephrased earlier manuscript item(s) D.2 into C.D2a. Thematically related to: D.1, T.4.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Separates evolution over time from transferring a fixed system to a new setting.

research_targets: Compare and calibrate forecasts across system changes

open_problems.title: Unclear effects of adopting AI
open_problems.description: Better task scores do not show what happens when people adopt an AI system. We need comparisons with realistic alternatives that estimate what adoption changes for users, workers and non-users, including who benefits or bears harms over time.

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem C.D3a not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: T.6b, P.3, D.1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Plain wording retains causation, distribution and time.

stakeholders: Workers, users, non-users and oversight bodies
research_targets: Identify adoption effects using credible comparisons and designs
Estimate effects across affected groups and time horizons

open_problems.title: Fragmented evidence about deployed AI
open_problems.description: Evidence about a system is spread across test reports, incident records and user observations. We need ways to combine these accounts so people can tell what they support, where they disagree, and what information is still missing for a decision.

lineage.what_changed: Rephrased earlier manuscript item(s) D.3 into C.D4b. Thematically related to: D.4, L.5.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Accessible Deployment issue about report synthesis, independent of monitoring design.

research_targets: Combine tests and operational evidence without masking conflicts

open_problems.title: Unclear when monitoring should trigger new tests
open_problems.description: After deployment, unexpected incidents and shifts in behaviour may reveal that earlier tests missed important risks. We need monitoring that can notice new problems and evidence for deciding when to reopen or expand an evaluation.

lineage.what_changed: Rephrased earlier manuscript item(s) D.4 into C.D4c. Thematically related to: D.3, L.3, I.1, I.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Accessible Deployment problem independently repairable from report synthesis.

research_targets: Test how monitoring identifies new failures and informs re-evaluation

open_problems.title: Limited anticipation of future capability needs
open_problems.description: New uses can require capabilities that existing tests do not assess. We need ways to forecast which capabilities future workflows will require and how far in advance those forecasts are reliable enough to guide evaluation planning.

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem C.D5 not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: D.2, T.1, T.4, P.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: A separate demand-side forecast if kept distinct from future system behaviour or building instruments.

research_targets: Backtest predictions of which capabilities future tasks will require

open_problems.title: Untraceable system and evidence changes
open_problems.description: A result applies to a particular system and procedure, yet both change over time. We need to trace versions, configurations, data and derived claims, and determine which evidence remains applicable after a change. Traceability must connect the evaluated object to the one actually used.

lineage.what_changed: Merged earlier manuscript items L.5, L.3 into R.L3. Thematically related to: D.3, D.4.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Clear Lifecycle problem across open and proprietary systems; prospective behaviour is Deployment. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in L.5, L.3 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Link a specific evaluation claim to its tested system, dependencies, data and configuration
Determine which evidence survives a specified configuration or procedure change and which needs retesting

open_problems.title: Inadequate access for independent verification
open_problems.description: Independent verification requires access appropriate to the claim, while unrestricted disclosure can compromise privacy, security and legitimate confidentiality. We need technical and procedural arrangements that expose sufficient evidence without creating unnecessary risks. The adequacy of access must itself be testable.

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from L.5 as R.L4. Thematically related to: L.4, I.2, I.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Clear Lifecycle technical access GP; capacity, authority and enforceable entitlements are institutional.

research_targets: Determine the minimum verification access required by different claim types
Assess how confidentiality and privacy protections change independent verification power

open_problems.title: Establishing whether evaluation evidence is independent of prior exposure
open_problems.description: How can evaluators detect exposure to test content during training, through tools or scaffolds, and during inference? They need to assess how exposure changes the interpretation of performance, including cases where the system’s training or retrieval history is only partly available.

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from L.1 as C.L.EXPOSURE. Thematically related to: T.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Well-scoped Lifecycle obstacle; distinct from selective reporting despite a common integrity umbrella.

research_targets: Detect and account for evaluation exposure across training and runtime channels

open_problems.title: Reproducing evaluations and the training evidence they depend on
open_problems.description: What records and tolerances let an independent team rerun inference and scoring, check whether an evaluation’s conclusions recur, and diagnose discrepancies? When a claim depends on how a model was trained, which training records or artifacts are also needed?

lineage.what_changed: Split earlier manuscript item(s) L.3 to form C.L.REPRODUCE. Thematically related to: L.5.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: A clear Lifecycle question as long as training artifacts are scoped to claims, not general training reproducibility. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in L.3 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Specify records and acceptable variation for reproducing a claim-bearing evaluation procedure
Identify when evaluation-relevant training histories and artifacts must be available to reconstruct evidence

open_problems.title: Making selective evaluation and reporting auditable
open_problems.description: How can evaluators account for the runs, prompts, benchmarks and analysis choices that produced a reported result? Preregistration, searchable evaluation records and clear explanations of exploratory changes should be assessed by whether they make selective evidence visible.

lineage.what_changed: Rephrased earlier manuscript item(s) L.2 into C.L.SELECTION. Thematically related to: V.2, T.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: One Lifecycle problem with an independent remedy from contamination. Preregistration is a response, not the definition.

research_targets: Audit the sampling, search and reporting choices that shaped the retained evaluation record

open_problems.title: Unclear rules connecting evidence to action
open_problems.description: Evidence does not determine action without rules about acceptable uncertainty, stakes and available alternatives. Institutions need defensible ways to connect findings and missing evidence to approval, restrictions, remediation or withdrawal. These rules must remain meaningful as systems and evaluation methods improve.

lineage.what_changed: Rephrased earlier manuscript item(s) I.1 into R.I1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: A single Institutions-level decision obstacle, with a plain seven-word title.

research_targets: Test evidence thresholds against different stakes, uncertainty and available actions
Compare reversible decision rules when material evidence is unavailable

open_problems.title: Unequal capacity to evaluate AI independently
open_problems.description: Independent evaluations require expertise, stable resources and facilities. Which arrangements let less-resourced groups run consequential evaluations and sustain their capacity as the systems and methods change?

lineage.what_changed: Merged earlier manuscript items I.2, L.4 into N.I2.capacity.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Sustainable institutional capacity has a different remedy from evaluator control over findings. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in I.2, L.4 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Test ways of broadening independent evaluation capability across institutions and regions

open_problems.title: Protecting the independence of AI evaluators
open_problems.description: Evaluators need discretion to set the scope, conduct tests and publish material findings when evaluated providers supply resources or models. Which funding and governance arrangements preserve that discretion across the evaluation process?

lineage.what_changed: Split earlier manuscript item(s) I.2 to form N.I2.independence. Thematically related to: I.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Focuses on one governance obstacle and gives a short, accessible framing. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in I.2 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Compare governance arrangements for independent agenda-setting and publication

open_problems.title: Enforcing rights to audit and challenge evaluations
open_problems.description: An independent auditor or affected group may need evidence that the evaluated provider controls. Which rights and review procedures make consequential claims auditable and contestable while respecting legitimate access restrictions?

lineage.what_changed: Split earlier manuscript item(s) I.3 to form N.I3.audit. Thematically related to: I.2.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: One clear institutional obstacle, distinct from technical implementation. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in I.3 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Compare enforceable audit access and challenge mechanisms against actual evidence needs

open_problems.title: Assigning responsibility for evaluation after deployment
open_problems.description: Different organizations may control the model, deployment, logs and capability to intervene. How should evaluation, incident reporting and response duties be allocated so emerging problems are detected and acted on?

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from I.3 as N.I3.duties. Thematically related to: D.4.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: One postdeployment institutional question distinct from technical monitoring and access.

research_targets: Evaluate duty allocation when several actors control the deployed system and its evidence

open_problems.title: Aligning incentives for informative AI evaluation
open_problems.description: Organizations can benefit from favorable tests or leave monitoring costs to others. Which incentives and cost-sharing arrangements lead to useful tests, candid reporting and sustained monitoring?

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from I.2 as N.I4.incentives. Thematically related to: I.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Unifies the original concerns around under-provision of informative evaluation.

research_targets: Compare coordination and cost-sharing designs for monitoring transparency
Test whether evaluation incentives reduce selective or low-information testing

open_problems.title: Missing voices in evaluation agendas
open_problems.description: Evaluation agendas can overlook those affected by AI who do not build or directly use it. We need ways for different forms of knowledge and underrepresented perspectives to influence question selection, concepts and interpretation. Participation must change consequential choices and remain open to disagreement.

lineage.what_changed: Split earlier manuscript item(s) P.2 to form R.P1.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Clear Purpose-level scope and readable title. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in P.2 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Test which forms of participation materially change agenda or metric decisions
Identify overlooked questions by comparing stakeholder priorities with evaluator agendas

open_problems.title: Misallocated evaluation effort
open_problems.description: No agenda can investigate every important question. We need principled ways to allocate effort across immediate harms, future risks, benefits and neglected evidence gaps. Priorities should consider decision value, irreversibility and uncertainty, while resisting the propensity to equate convenient tests or abundant publications with importance.

lineage.what_changed: Rephrased earlier manuscript item(s) P.1 into R.P3. Thematically related to: P.2.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: A clear Purpose-level problem about the evaluation portfolio.

research_targets: Compare prioritization rules using decision value, irreversibility, uncertainty and resource constraints

open_problems.title: Accounting for delayed and indirect evaluation outcomes
open_problems.description: Short evaluation windows can leave effects on non-users, future users and resource use outside the decision. Which indirect and delayed outcomes should be included, and when do practical proxies misrepresent them?

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from P.3 as N.P2.horizons.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: General Purpose framing; downstream causal estimation and effects on the agenda remain separate.

research_targets: Compare which indirect and delayed outcomes enter evaluation boundaries and how proxies affect decisions

open_problems.title: Making conflicting values visible in evaluation
open_problems.description: People can disagree about what an AI system should achieve, whose outcomes should count, and which trade-offs are acceptable. How can evaluations reflect those differences, including effects on autonomy, without hiding them in one summary score?

lineage.what_changed: Split earlier manuscript item(s) P.3 to form N.P2.values.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: One coherent Purpose-level question with accessible wording. [Action required: Human co-author must confirm what specific defect or overlap in P.3 justifies this restructuring.]

research_targets: Compare representations of conflicting values without hiding distributional trade-offs
Test agency-sensitive criteria against throughput-only indicators

open_problems.title: Detecting blind spots in AI-assisted evaluation agendas
open_problems.description: AI can help discover, phrase and prioritize evaluation questions, changing which concerns get attention. How can people detect systematic omissions across agenda revisions and decide when to revise the selection process?

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem N.P4.agenda not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: P.2, T.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: Coherent Purpose-level obstacle aligned to the paper’s distinctive thesis.

research_targets: Detect systematic omissions from AI-assisted selection over successive agenda cycles

open_problems.title: Benchmark incentives and the direction of AI development
open_problems.description: Published benchmarks can direct effort towards measured targets and away from other capabilities or impacts. How can evaluators identify such shifts and judge whether they represent useful progress?

lineage.what_changed: Retained or adapted from T.3 as N.P4.benchmarks.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: One general Purpose-level mechanism, separate from who sets an evaluation agenda.

research_targets: Measure causal changes in development priorities after evaluative signals are introduced

open_problems.title: Testing whether AI confidence is trustworthy
open_problems.description: An AI system may express confidence or defer to a person without having a well-defined probability of being correct. How can evaluators check whether these signals track reliability for different tasks and populations, including after conditions change?

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem G.V.CALIBRATION not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: V.1, V.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: One Validity obstacle with a plain six-word title. C.V3a instead assesses uncertainty in evaluation estimates.

research_targets: Validate output confidence and abstention across task types, levels of granularity and shifts

open_problems.title: Comparing performance under unequal resource use
open_problems.description: Models can obtain similar scores using different amounts of training, inference, tools and human support. How should evaluations record these inputs and compare performance under comparable constraints, so apparent gains can be distinguished from additional resource use?

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem G.T.RESOURCES not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: T.5, T.1, F.5.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: A recurring Techniques obstacle that applies beyond one benchmark and has a concise title.

research_targets: Validate resource boundaries, reporting and performance–cost comparisons for different evaluation configurations

open_problems.title: Validating evaluations across languages and communities
open_problems.description: A test that works in one language or community can change meaning when it is translated or reused. What evidence can distinguish a real performance gap from a shift in the task, reference answers or local expectations, and when is a new test needed?

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem G.V.LOCAL not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: V.1, P.3.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: A Validity general problem about transport of measurement meaning, spanning multiple tasks and groups.

research_targets: Validate criteria for choosing translation, cultural adaptation, or local reconstruction of an evaluation
Test competing explanations and document evidence for interpretations

open_problems.title: Making AI evaluation indicators useful to the public
open_problems.description: Public indicators need to make results from many tests understandable while retaining what was tested, how widely a capability is used, and where the evidence is weak. Which summaries help non-specialists interpret changes and use the evidence in decisions?

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem G.D.INDICATORS not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: D.3, P.2.
lineage.why_changed: Clarity & scope rationale: An interpretable reporting problem across uses, distinct from the statistical construction of an individual test score.

research_targets: Test public summaries of AI evaluation for comprehension, comparability and decision usefulness
Combine tests and operational evidence without masking conflicts

open_problems.title: Keeping shared evaluation standards current
open_problems.description: Evaluation standards must evolve as systems and methods change, while institutions still need to compare results obtained under earlier rules. Who should revise shared standards, and what evidence and transition procedures make changes timely and interpretable?

lineage.what_changed: Proposed new open problem G.I.STANDARDS not directly present as a standalone item in the Nov 6 draft. Thematically related to: I.1, I.3.

C.F1a.title: Unclear boundaries of evaluated systems
C.F1a.description: A model, its tools and the people using it can jointly determine what happens. Evaluators need rules for deciding what belongs to the system a claim covers, and when evidence about one component applies to the whole.
research_targets: Define and test claims over explicit system boundaries
Establish when component-level evidence warrants a system-level claim within a specified system boundary

C.F2a.title: Unclear definitions of abilities and tendencies
C.F2a.description: A test score alone cannot tell us what an AI system can do or what it tends to do in practice. We need definitions that distinguish these properties and can be revised when new evidence about behaviour or its causes disagrees with them.
research_targets: Connect ability and tendency definitions to evidence across contexts

C.F3a.title: Scores lack a shared meaning across tests
C.F3a.description: A higher score may reflect a different test, population or difficulty rather than a more capable system. Evaluators need defensible scales for comparing results and describing how broadly abilities apply, including when systems exceed existing tests.
research_targets: Identify invariant scales and legitimate limits of comparisons
Separate breadth and difficulty from instrument-specific thresholds

C.F4a.title: Limits on what evaluation can establish
C.F4a.description: Some systems can look identical in every test evaluators can run while behaving differently elsewhere. We need to know which claims can be settled with the observations, interventions and resources available, and what extra evidence would change the answer.
research_targets: Map identifiability limits under stated access and resource conditions

R.T2.title: Weak experimental control and causal diagnosis
R.T2.description: The same outcome can arise from very different mechanisms. Evaluation needs controlled comparisons and interventions that separate model, scaffold, human and environmental contributions. The open problem is to obtain explanations useful for diagnosis while retaining realistic conditions and accounting for interactions between components.
research_targets: Separate causal contributions of models, scaffolds, humans and environments using evaluation interventions
Establish fair and realistic comparisons against feasible human and human–AI workflows

R.T5.title: Unsafe or unfaithful evaluation environments
R.T5.description: A test environment must reveal relevant behaviour while containing harm and protecting participants. Sandboxes, simulated users and human studies can alter the phenomenon they are meant to study. We need environments whose safety constraints, realism and remaining distortions are explicit and experimentally examinable.
research_targets: Determine which environment constraints preserve relevant behaviour while proportionately containing harm
Determine how to protect participants and annotators while maintaining credible behavioural evidence

C.T.BASELINE.title: Choosing fair and realistic human and human–AI baselines
C.T.BASELINE.description: What comparison workflow, participant experience, resource budget and prior access make human, AI and hybrid performance meaningfully comparable? The evaluation must distinguish an artificial control from the best feasible alternative available to the people making the decision.
research_targets: Establish fair and realistic comparisons against feasible human and human–AI workflows

C.T.ELICIT.title: Eliciting consequential behaviour under known conditions
C.T.ELICIT.description: How can evaluation procedures reveal consequential capabilities, tendencies and failures under a specified system configuration and resource budget? We need evidence that the evaluation gave the system a suitable opportunity to act and that the test conditions did not substitute a different capability for the one of interest.
research_targets: Design elicitation methods that separate behaviour revealed from assumptions about resources and opportunities
Identify how testing changes behaviour and bound that distortion in evaluation design
Design and compare tests for discovering meaningful rare failure modes under stated operating conditions

C.T.RARE.title: Discovering rare but consequential failures
C.T.RARE.description: How can evaluators choose scenarios, observation horizons and stress conditions that are informative about rare failure modes in a specified domain of use? Tests need to surface meaningful failures and near misses without confusing discovery coverage with estimates of how frequently the failures occur.
research_targets: Design and compare tests for discovering meaningful rare failure modes under stated operating conditions

C.T.REACTIVITY.title: Testing changes the behaviour it is meant to measure
C.T.REACTIVITY.description: How can evaluators tell when a system behaves differently because it is being tested, and design comparisons that estimate the resulting distortion? The challenge includes changes caused by the testing protocol itself as well as changes when a system recognises the evaluation context.
research_targets: Identify how testing changes behaviour and bound that distortion in evaluation design

C.T.TIMELY.title: Developing and maintaining tests in time for emerging capabilities
C.T.TIMELY.description: How can evaluators prepare, validate and refresh instruments in time to assess emerging capabilities under limited compute and expert time? Adaptive task selection and benchmark repair need to preserve coverage and meaningful discrimination as systems and uses change.
research_targets: Determine how to preserve test coverage, discrimination and verifiability within a fixed budget
Design, validate and maintain tests in time for emerging capability changes

C.V1a.title: Scores can support the wrong conclusions
C.V1a.description: An evaluation score can reflect shortcuts or features of the test instead of the ability or risk it is meant to measure. Evaluators need to show which conclusions a result supports, for which people or settings, and what evidence rules out other explanations.
research_targets: Test competing explanations and document evidence for interpretations

C.V3a.title: Overconfidence in rankings and risk estimates
C.V3a.description: Small or repeatedly selected samples can make model rankings unstable and rare failures hard to estimate. Evaluators need uncertainty estimates that reflect how tests were collected and show which conclusions hold across groups, including where the evidence is too sparse to tell.
stakeholders: Oversight bodies and people exposed to harms
research_targets: Calibrate uncertainty under dependence, selection and heterogeneity
Design and validate estimates for rare-event rates and uncertainty

C.V4a.title: Weak assurance about AI system behaviour
C.V4a.description: Passing tests does not establish that a failure is impossible. Formal checks may establish properties of parts of a decision process under stated assumptions. We need ways to assess what tests and proofs jointly establish and what uncertainty remains.
stakeholders: Deployers, oversight bodies and people exposed to harms
research_targets: Derive bounded assurance accounting for coverage and search limits
Compare formal guarantees with empirical checks of assumptions and scope

C.V6.title: Limited formal assurance for AI decisions
C.V6.description: Formal checks can establish some properties of a specified decision process, but an AI system may include learned components and changing surroundings. Which parts can be checked, how can we test the assumptions, and what conclusions apply to the complete system?
research_targets: Compare formal guarantees with empirical checks of assumptions and scope

C.V7.title: Unreliable judges and evaluation methods
C.V7.description: When tests and judges use similar models or data, they can agree while sharing the same errors. We need ways to check difficult answers against trustworthy standards and to test whether whole evaluation methods work, using evidence independent of the systems being evaluated.
stakeholders: Evaluators and users of evaluation results
research_targets: Develop and calibrate reference standards for hard-to-judge work
Test evaluator reliability with independent evidence and controls

R.D1.title: Weak prediction beyond tested conditions
R.D1.description: Evaluation is useful when it informs behaviour in conditions that were not directly tested. We need models of how results transfer across tasks, users, interfaces and operational settings. These predictions must identify their assumptions and failure conditions rather than treating a benchmark score as a universal deployment forecast.
research_targets: Validate transfer models against held-out operational conditions

C.D2a.title: Forecasts break when AI systems change
C.D2a.description: Tests of current systems give only partial evidence about later models or systems that learn during use. We need forecasts that state what changes they assume, how far ahead they apply, and how their uncertainty changes when the system evolves in other ways.
research_targets: Compare and calibrate forecasts across system changes

C.D3a.title: Unclear effects of adopting AI
C.D3a.description: Better task scores do not show what happens when people adopt an AI system. We need comparisons with realistic alternatives that estimate what adoption changes for users, workers and non-users, including who benefits or bears harms over time.
stakeholders: Workers, users, non-users and oversight bodies
research_targets: Identify adoption effects using credible comparisons and designs
Estimate effects across affected groups and time horizons

C.D4b.title: Fragmented evidence about deployed AI
C.D4b.description: Evidence about a system is spread across test reports, incident records and user observations. We need ways to combine these accounts so people can tell what they support, where they disagree, and what information is still missing for a decision.
research_targets: Combine tests and operational evidence without masking conflicts

C.D4c.title: Unclear when monitoring should trigger new tests
C.D4c.description: After deployment, unexpected incidents and shifts in behaviour may reveal that earlier tests missed important risks. We need monitoring that can notice new problems and evidence for deciding when to reopen or expand an evaluation.
research_targets: Test how monitoring identifies new failures and informs re-evaluation

C.D5.title: Limited anticipation of future capability needs
C.D5.description: New uses can require abilities that existing tests do not assess. We need ways to forecast which abilities future workflows will require and how far in advance those forecasts are reliable enough to guide evaluation planning.
research_targets: Backtest predictions of which capabilities future tasks will require

R.L3.title: Untraceable system and evidence changes
R.L3.description: A result applies to a particular system and procedure, yet both change over time. We need to trace versions, configurations, data and derived claims, and determine which evidence remains applicable after a change. Traceability must connect the evaluated object to the one actually used.
research_targets: Link a specific evaluation claim to its tested system, dependencies, data and configuration
Determine which evidence survives a specified configuration or procedure change and which needs retesting

R.L4.title: Inadequate access for independent verification
R.L4.description: Independent verification requires access appropriate to the claim, while unrestricted disclosure can compromise privacy, security and legitimate confidentiality. We need technical and procedural arrangements that expose sufficient evidence without creating unnecessary risks. The adequacy of access must itself be testable.
research_targets: Determine the minimum verification access required by different claim types
Assess how confidentiality and privacy protections change independent verification power

C.L.EXPOSURE.title: Establishing whether evaluation evidence is independent of prior exposure
C.L.EXPOSURE.description: How can evaluators detect exposure to test content during training, through tools or scaffolds, and during inference? They need to assess how exposure changes the interpretation of performance, including cases where the system’s training or retrieval history is only partly available.
research_targets: Detect and account for evaluation exposure across training and runtime channels

C.L.REPRODUCE.title: Reproducing evaluations and the training evidence they depend on
C.L.REPRODUCE.description: What records and tolerances let an independent team rerun inference and scoring, check whether an evaluation’s conclusions recur, and diagnose discrepancies? When a claim depends on how a model was trained, which training records or artifacts are also needed?
research_targets: Specify records and acceptable variation for reproducing a claim-bearing evaluation procedure
Identify when evaluation-relevant training histories and artifacts must be available to reconstruct evidence

C.L.SELECTION.title: Making selective evaluation and reporting auditable
C.L.SELECTION.description: How can evaluators account for the runs, prompts, benchmarks and analysis choices that produced a reported result? Preregistration, searchable evaluation records and clear explanations of exploratory changes should be assessed by whether they make selective evidence visible.
research_targets: Audit the sampling, search and reporting choices that shaped the retained evaluation record

R.I1.title: Unclear rules connecting evidence to action
R.I1.description: Evidence does not determine action without rules about acceptable uncertainty, stakes and available alternatives. Institutions need defensible ways to connect findings and missing evidence to approval, restrictions, remediation or withdrawal. These rules must remain meaningful as systems and evaluation methods improve.
research_targets: Test evidence thresholds against different stakes, uncertainty and available actions
Compare reversible decision rules when material evidence is unavailable

N.I2.capacity.title: Unequal capacity to evaluate AI independently
N.I2.capacity.description: Independent evaluations require expertise, stable resources and facilities. Which arrangements let less-resourced groups run consequential evaluations and sustain their capacity as the systems and methods change?
research_targets: Test ways of broadening independent evaluation capability across institutions and regions

N.I2.independence.title: Protecting the independence of AI evaluators
N.I2.independence.description: Evaluators need discretion to set the scope, conduct tests and publish material findings when evaluated providers supply resources or models. Which funding and governance arrangements preserve that discretion across the evaluation process?
research_targets: Compare governance arrangements for independent agenda-setting and publication

N.I3.audit.title: Enforcing rights to audit and challenge evaluations
N.I3.audit.description: An independent auditor or affected group may need evidence that the evaluated provider controls. Which rights and review procedures make consequential claims auditable and contestable while respecting legitimate access restrictions?
research_targets: Compare enforceable audit access and challenge mechanisms against actual evidence needs

N.I3.duties.title: Assigning responsibility for evaluation after deployment
N.I3.duties.description: Different organizations may control the model, deployment, logs and ability to intervene. How should evaluation, incident reporting and response duties be allocated so emerging problems are detected and acted on?
research_targets: Evaluate duty allocation when several actors control the deployed system and its evidence

N.I4.incentives.title: Aligning incentives for informative AI evaluation
N.I4.incentives.description: Organizations can benefit from favorable tests or leave monitoring costs to others. Which incentives and cost-sharing arrangements lead to useful tests, candid reporting and sustained monitoring?
research_targets: Compare coordination and cost-sharing designs for monitoring transparency
Test whether evaluation incentives reduce selective or low-information testing

R.P1.title: Missing voices in evaluation agendas
R.P1.description: Evaluation agendas can overlook those affected by AI who do not build or directly use it. We need ways for different forms of knowledge and underrepresented perspectives to influence question selection, concepts and interpretation. Participation must change consequential choices and remain open to disagreement.
research_targets: Test which forms of participation materially change agenda or metric decisions
Identify overlooked questions by comparing stakeholder priorities with evaluator agendas

R.P3.title: Misallocated evaluation effort
R.P3.description: No agenda can investigate every important question. We need principled ways to allocate effort across immediate harms, future risks, benefits and neglected evidence gaps. Priorities should consider decision value, irreversibility and uncertainty, while resisting the tendency to equate convenient tests or abundant publications with importance.
research_targets: Compare prioritization rules using decision value, irreversibility, uncertainty and resource constraints

N.P2.horizons.title: Accounting for delayed and indirect evaluation outcomes
N.P2.horizons.description: Short evaluation windows can leave effects on non-users, future users and resource use outside the decision. Which indirect and delayed outcomes should be included, and when do practical proxies misrepresent them?
research_targets: Compare which indirect and delayed outcomes enter evaluation boundaries and how proxies affect decisions

N.P2.values.title: Making conflicting values visible in evaluation
N.P2.values.description: People can disagree about what an AI system should achieve, whose outcomes should count, and which trade-offs are acceptable. How can evaluations reflect those differences, including effects on autonomy, without hiding them in one summary score?
research_targets: Compare representations of conflicting values without hiding distributional trade-offs
Test agency-sensitive criteria against throughput-only indicators

N.P4.agenda.title: Detecting blind spots in AI-assisted evaluation agendas
N.P4.agenda.description: AI can help discover, phrase and prioritize evaluation questions, changing which concerns get attention. How can people detect systematic omissions across agenda revisions and decide when to revise the selection process?
research_targets: Detect systematic omissions from AI-assisted selection over successive agenda cycles

N.P4.benchmarks.title: Benchmark incentives and the direction of AI development
N.P4.benchmarks.description: Published benchmarks can direct effort towards measured targets and away from other capabilities or impacts. How can evaluators identify such shifts and judge whether they represent useful progress?
research_targets: Measure causal changes in development priorities after evaluative signals are introduced

G.V.CALIBRATION.title: Testing whether AI confidence is trustworthy
G.V.CALIBRATION.description: An AI system may express confidence or defer to a person without having a well-defined probability of being correct. How can evaluators check whether these signals track reliability for different tasks and populations, including after conditions change?
research_targets: Validate output confidence and abstention across task types, levels of granularity and shifts

G.T.RESOURCES.title: Comparing performance under unequal resource use
G.T.RESOURCES.description: Models can obtain similar scores using different amounts of training, inference, tools and human support. How should evaluations record these inputs and compare performance under comparable constraints, so apparent gains can be distinguished from additional resource use?
research_targets: Validate resource boundaries, reporting and performance–cost comparisons for different evaluation configurations

G.V.LOCAL.title: Validating evaluations across languages and communities
G.V.LOCAL.description: A test that works in one language or community can change meaning when it is translated or reused. What evidence can distinguish a real performance gap from a shift in the task, reference answers or local expectations, and when is a new test needed?
research_targets: Validate criteria for choosing translation, cultural adaptation, or local reconstruction of an evaluation
Test competing explanations and document evidence for interpretations

G.D.INDICATORS.title: Making AI evaluation indicators useful to the public
G.D.INDICATORS.description: Public indicators need to make results from many tests understandable while retaining what was tested, how widely a capability is used, and where the evidence is weak. Which summaries help non-specialists interpret changes and use the evidence in decisions?
research_targets: Test public summaries of AI evaluation for comprehension, comparability and decision usefulness
Combine tests and operational evidence without masking conflicts

G.I.STANDARDS.title: Keeping shared evaluation standards current
G.I.STANDARDS.description: Evaluation standards must evolve as systems and methods change, while institutions still need to compare results obtained under earlier rules. Who should revise shared standards, and what evidence and transition procedures make changes timely and interpretable?
research_targets: Compare institutional revision and transition mechanisms for shared evaluation standards

G.V.PORTFOLIO.title: Combining tests without repeating their blind spots
G.V.PORTFOLIO.description: An evaluation may combine several tests, but they can rely on the same assumptions or miss the same behaviours. How can evaluators decide whether a new method adds independent evidence and identify which uncertainties still limit the combined claim?
research_targets: Test method complementarity and shared blind spots when combining evaluation evidence

M.T.SOCIAL.title: Tests miss behaviour with unfamiliar AI partners
M.T.SOCIAL.description: Agents may cooperate well with familiar partners and fail when the mix changes. We need tests across partner populations and roles that reveal which behaviours transfer, which depend on shared conventions, and which failures only appear at the group level.
research_targets: Measure behaviours that emerge from interaction among humans and AI systems or among AI systems
Test population-dependent collective behaviour with held-out partners and roles

M.T.HUMAN.title: Tests miss how human–AI teams change
M.T.HUMAN.description: AI assistance can improve a team’s immediate output while changing how people understand a task, rely on advice or develop skills. Evaluations need to observe people and AI working together over time and check whether simulated users capture the responses that matter.
stakeholders: Users and workers in AI-assisted teams
research_targets: Measure behaviours that emerge from interaction among humans and AI systems or among AI systems
Design longitudinal tests for behaviour that changes with interaction history, adaptation or learning
Design repeated human–AI studies that distinguish performance from changes in human understanding and reliance

M.P.PRIORITIES.title: Agreed priorities get lost in evaluation practice
M.P.PRIORITIES.description: People can agree on what matters and still receive tests or reports that answer different questions. We need ways to check whether priorities survive the choice of claims, measures and reported results, and to make departures visible to those affected.
research_targets: Audit whether agreed priorities are retained across claims, measures and reported outcomes

generation_method.title: How the mixed-source questions were generated
generation_method.overview: The workflow turns source material into editorial candidate versions, then tests alternative sets against a frozen rubric and coverage model. A recommended set goes to coauthors for judgment.

stages.title: Collect and trace
stages.text: Compile published sources, Programme questions and manuscript entries. Track source questions and locators separately from editorial interpretations.

stages.title: Draft candidate versions
stages.text: Carry forward 67 versions and add six from Programme gaps and three from manuscript framing. Record variant families, conflicts and provenance.

stages.title: Score and map coverage
stages.text: Apply the five-criterion rubric and code each candidate’s coverage of distinct stakeholder needs and research targets as 0, 0.5 or 1.

stages.title: Select sets at specified sizes
stages.text: Solve the model at each feasible size. Compare the same-size results on the same coverage dictionary and bring alternatives to human review.

sourceExample.citation: Anwar et al., Foundational Challenges in Assuring Alignment and Safety of Large Language Models
sourceExample.explanation: The paper question concerns defining capabilities. The revised general problem also distinguishes abilities from tendencies and asks how evidence should revise those definitions.

objective.formula: F = 20 × (mean(Q1)/4 + mean(Q2)/4 + mean(Q3)/4 + weighted need coverage + weighted research coverage)
objective.coverage: For each unit, take the maximum credit among the selected candidates. Multiply by the unit weight, sum, and divide by the total weight in that ledger.
objective.roles: Q1 is relevance, Q2 openness and Q3 clarity and category fit. Q4 and Q5 diagnose stakeholder impact and research value. Their portfolio counterparts are the two coverage ledgers.
objective.eligibility: Require Q1≥3, Q2≥2 and Q3≥2. A documented Q2=1 exception requires Q4≥3. All 76 versions passed without using that exception.

algorithm.constraints: Select exactly K eligible versions, at least one in each category, with no shared canonical parent or named pairwise conflict.
algorithm.search: The solver branches on inclusion or exclusion, removes infeasible branches and uses upper bounds on remaining item scores and obtainable coverage to prune the search. It works on an exact integer scale.
algorithm.scale: For the baseline objective, L = lcm(4K, 2W_need, 2W_research), where W denotes a ledger’s total weight. Convert integer units to points by multiplying by 20 and dividing by L.
tieBreak: Higher mean Q1 at fixed K

limits: The historical K=48 result is an exact recommendation for a specified objective and frozen candidate pool. The manuscript’s approximately 35-question target motivates a separate size scenario for author review.

All 17 new coverage units are exclusive to newly introduced candidates under the current coding. The bridge comparison tests the numerical effect of removing those units. An independent cross-review of all candidate–unit links would test the coding.
Openness scores express editorial judgments. A current literature review should record what existing work solves, under which assumptions and what remains unresolved.
The source trail distinguishes extracts, paraphrases, thematic links and newly written formulations. Several related records can belong to the same evidence family.
nextChecks: Set the manuscript length before choosing a portfolio. Compare K=35 and K=36 at the same coverage weights and take the replacements to author review.
Cross-rate every candidate against the expanded ledger. Record each full, partial or unsupported link before rerunning with the old and expanded ledgers.
Use current primary research to review openness. For each disputed problem, record what has been solved, the assumptions, the residual obstacle and reviewer agreement or disagreement.
Preserve explicit source-question IDs and source roles when formulating candidates. Record independent verification separately from related material and shared provenance.
Check that descriptions fit the intended manuscript layout and invite readers to assess clarity. Line count varies with the typesetting.

scope.selected_portfolio: Frozen 48-question portfolio chosen from 76 candidate versions. The latest manuscript and the older comparison baseline have separate version identities.
scope.audit_type: Targeted inspection of source membership, representative source joins, rendered and underlying evidence layers, and release boundaries.
scope.limits: Counts and inspected joins are reproducible. Broader extraction recall, candidate interpretation, openness, scores, and reviewer agreement require separate assessment.

findings.observed: Latest manuscript Table 2, p. 11, adds a single source to the 26-row comparison baseline, Dhar, Peng and Søgaard. The extraction registry records the earlier membership and contains no Dhar records.
findings.correction: Version the two Table 2 lists separately. Show Dhar as a newly added source with a post-freeze concern ledger. A rerun with new evidence would need its own run ID.

findings.observed: The rerun integrates 67 frozen candidate versions, the Programme crosswalk, manuscript lineage and nine added versions. The literature panel exposes 1,022 older Table 2 registry records through a display adapter. The solver input is the assembled 76-version pool.
findings.correction: Describe the registry as an earlier audit and evidence layer. Describe the rerun as operating on the curated pool and its recorded evidence. State that exact optimization verifies selection under the encoded rubric, constraints and scores.

findings.topic: Source IDs versus author question numbers
findings.observed: Bank Q90 refers to Schmidt Sciences on estimating rare failures, while Anwar et al. v2 printed question 90 is bank Q572. Bank Q202 refers to Sharkey et al. on feature overlap, while Anwar et al. v2 printed question 202 is bank Q683.
findings.correction: Join using the typed registry ID and the source ID, pinned version and locator. Render the registry ID and printed author question number with distinct labels.

findings.topic: Evidence scope for the AI-assisted agenda question
findings.observed: N.P4.agenda lists seven reference strings from four Chen et al. bank records, Q50, Q51, Q63 and Q64. The source discusses the reciprocal influence of evaluations and AI development. The illustrative formulation R.P4.Q2 was an editorial synthesis.
findings.correction: Mark the longitudinal question about omissions in AI-assisted agenda setting as an editorial proposal. Group Chen et al. as one related source family. A human–agent interaction experiment can provide a bounded comparator on influence over analytical judgments, with its separate study setting and post-audit citation status.

findings.topic: Related evidence for the scope question
findings.observed: The illustrative formulations R.F1.Q1 and R.F1.Q2 for C.F1a are recorded editorial syntheses. Anwar et al. question 53 (bank Q535), Chen et al. §1e (Q05), and two multi-agent evaluation and governance passages (Q468 and Q476) support specific scope or composition facets.
findings.correction: Record the broad question as a synthesis. Attribute tool permissions, factor attribution and multi-agent composition to the relevant source locators as distinct motivating facets.

findings.observed: In the inspected run, all 144 selected primary links and 39 selected new-candidate links have reverse metadata. Of 308 selected-target secondary links, 296 lack separate reverse candidate metadata. The source and candidate views derive links from different arrays.
findings.correction: Derive a separately labeled reverse index for secondary thematic matches. Preserve direct, partial, and related-variant distinctions. Thematic fit was judged in the audit and does not identify the historical origin of a manuscript problem.

findings.observed: The generic reference list includes 29 separately prefixed Programme references across six selected versions and five separately prefixed internal feedback references across five selected versions. These are also handled by dedicated evidence views.
findings.correction: Replace prefix filtering with typed evidence groups. Use unique source/version/locator keys for display and retain each distinct supported facet.

findings.observed: Twenty-two of 26 earlier Table 2 sources supply registry records. The public Programme page, Stanford AI Measurement Science center page and two Coefficient Giving pages have zero question-level registry records. The 208 additions to the earlier assembled Table 2 archive include expansions of source facets, which may overlap semantically. All earlier Table 2 records have locators and a pending human verification status.
findings.correction: Report covered sources, question records, formulation representatives and conceptual families separately. Keep source-level inclusion, locator checks, extraction review and substantive relevance in separate fields. Track the separate 291-prompt Programme corpus under its own version and access class.

findings.observed: The older manuscript describes collective expert-led synthesis with Programme, faculty discussion and forward-looking sources. The crosswalk captures where old themes or prose carry into revised questions. Topic overlap and writing assignments do not identify the origin or author of individual old questions.
findings.correction: Label versioned draft lineage as retain, reframe, split, merge, extension, or new. Record a specific contributor or source as historical origin only with explicit provenance.

findings.observed: The standalone review file embeds original draft, Programme, feedback, source extraction and candidate information in its serialized data. The reproducibility files can carry the corresponding internal source records.
findings.correction: Build a separate public export using a field allowlist after project approval. Check the actual packaged files and serialized data, including records hidden by the UI.

findings.observed: The recorded feedback consists of two excerpted notes and one supplied paraphrase of an email. Public papers on controlled training or evaluation workflows can support bounded technical claims about those methods.
findings.correction: Keep feedback and associated deck or email material private. Cite public technical comparators at their own versioned locators and label them independently of internal feedback.

findings.observed: The public capability indicators report and a portion of the Programme material overlap in project leadership and subject matter. Multiple course items and source strings can reflect one underlying evidence family.
findings.correction: Record related inputs under an evidence-family ID. Treat indicator comprehension and decision usefulness as empirical questions, separate from the existence of a reporting framework.

source.title: On Challenges in Evaluation Methodology: A Review
source.source_locator: §2 and Figure 3 for method and taxonomy, §§3–6 for concern descriptions, §7 for the recency and checklist analyses

dhar.evidence_type: Post-freeze thematic ledger. The source defines methodological concerns, and the proposed questions are new AI-assisted editorial formulations derived from those themes.

corpus_scope.summary: NLP-centered scoping review. The authors formed the taxonomy through iterative manual review, used LLM-assisted coding of papers, and manually checked final annotations.

limitations: The source surveys a bounded corpus. Recency or checklist coverage provides evidence of attention within that scope.
Current openness, independent priority and suitability for a general-problem portfolio remain unassessed.
The concerns overlap with existing themes and differ in granularity. The 22 entries are evidence candidates rather than 22 independent new general problems.
