concerns.label: Coverage of the intended construct
concerns.proposed_question: How can evaluators check whether AI-generated tasks represent the intended capability and its important subskills?

concerns.label: Quality of reference answers
concerns.proposed_question: When AI proposes reference answers, how can expert review distinguish labeling mistakes from legitimate disagreement?

concerns.label: Incidental cues in test items
concerns.proposed_question: How can evaluators detect superficial cues in AI-generated items that let systems score well without the intended ability?

concerns.label: Prior exposure to test content
concerns.proposed_question: How can auditors estimate whether benchmark items or close variants appeared in the training or development of the evaluated system or its AI judge?

concerns.label: Partitions matched to the target use
concerns.proposed_question: How should item generation, tuning, and held-out testing be partitioned so that reported generalization matches the intended use?

concerns.label: Typical cases and targeted stress tests
concerns.proposed_question: How should evaluators combine representative samples and AI-generated stress cases while keeping deployment-frequency estimates interpretable?

concerns.label: Observed success and explanatory accounts
concerns.proposed_question: How can evaluators pair results on AI-generated tests with independent evidence about which linguistic or reasoning competence produced success?

concerns.label: Prediction of practical outcomes
concerns.proposed_question: When do improvements on AI-assisted evaluation metrics predict better outcomes for people using the system?

concerns.label: Sensitivity to meaningful linguistic differences
concerns.proposed_question: How can an AI-assisted scorer recognize meaningful semantic differences and credit valid alternative expressions?

concerns.label: Quality of human judgments
concerns.proposed_question: How can teams test whether human judgments remain reliable and valid when AI assists raters with rubrics, examples, or preliminary scores?

concerns.label: Dependence on the evaluation data
concerns.proposed_question: How stable is an AI-assisted metric when references, datasets, languages, and sample sizes change while the intended construct is held fixed?

concerns.label: Transfer of metrics across tasks
concerns.proposed_question: What evidence should justify reusing an AI scoring rule on tasks with different objectives or difficulty structures?

concerns.label: Dependence on the systems being scored
concerns.proposed_question: How can evaluator teams measure and account for judge preferences tied to the evaluated model’s family, writing style, or output order?

concerns.label: Comparable metric definitions and protocols
concerns.proposed_question: Which parts of AI-assisted scoring protocols should be shared to enable comparisons, and where is use-specific adaptation needed?

concerns.label: Choice of decision-relevant claims
concerns.proposed_question: How can stakeholder goals and value judgments be made explicit when AI helps propose hypotheses for an evaluation?

concerns.label: Bounds on claims supported by tasks
concerns.proposed_question: How can reviewers determine which system-level claims are warranted by the specific tasks in an AI-assisted evaluation?

concerns.label: Validity of statistical inference
concerns.proposed_question: How should comparisons account for correlated generated items, repeated AI judgments, and testing across many metrics?

concerns.label: Power, uncertainty, and thresholds
concerns.proposed_question: How should teams choose sample sizes, meaningful effect sizes, and thresholds when item generation and judgment both add uncertainty?

concerns.label: Control of comparison confounds
concerns.proposed_question: How can matched or factorial comparisons separate model improvements from changes in scaffolding, resources, or AI-assisted grading?

concerns.label: Interpretation of leaderboard movement
concerns.proposed_question: How should leaderboards report uncertainty and adaptation to repeated AI-assisted testing so rank movement supports defensible claims?

concerns.label: Disclosure needed to interpret results
concerns.proposed_question: What should evaluators disclose about AI-generated items, automated judges, scoring choices, budgets, and failures so readers can interpret the results?

concerns.label: Independent reruns and checks
concerns.proposed_question: Which versioned artifacts and access arrangements enable independent reruns and detect shared software or judge failures in AI-assisted evaluations?

baseline.manuscriptTarget: Approximately 35 general problems, with a short heading and a description understandable to AI stakeholders
baseline.headingCheck: All 48 headings have fewer than ten space-delimited words.
baseline.descriptionCheck: Current descriptions range from 26 to 48 words. The manuscript layout determines whether they fit in three or four lines.
baseline.reviewLimit: This is an editorial scope and boundary audit. Current openness requires separate evidence review and collective author decisions.

rules.label: Evaluation-specific scope
rules.text: Name the evaluation claim, behavioural indicator or societal impact, the evidence gap and the decision it affects. AI design and general governance are neighbouring topics unless tied to how evaluation evidence is produced or used.

rules.label: One independent research obstacle
rules.text: A general problem should recur across situations. When two descriptions seem close, ask whether solving one could leave the other unresolved. Use a secondary category for a genuine cross-link.

rules.label: Substantive evidence
rules.text: Identify current partial solutions, their assumptions and the unresolved obstacle. Source links and numerical openness ratings guide review.

rules.label: Scope-preserving copyedit
rules.text: Retain the existing scores and coverage when a wording edit leaves the claim, evidence obligation, affected decision and category unchanged. Check semantic equivalence before carrying the frozen scores forward.

rules.label: New version and rescoring
rules.text: A narrower or expanded claim, a different category, or a new merge or split requires revised rationale and affected scores, coverage links and conflicts. Preserve both versions until authors decide.

rules.label: Previously scored alternative
rules.text: An unchanged alternative already in the frozen pool can be compared using its existing scores and tags. A new inclusion constraint changes the optimization and calls for a separate replay.

categories.label: Foundations
categories.assessment: The four questions concern evaluation units, constructs, scales and limits in principle. Distinguish defining a system from attributing the result to a component, and defining a shared scale from estimating uncertainty on that scale.

categories.label: Techniques
categories.assessment: These concern producing evidence through design, controls, realistic conditions, resource matching, interactions and timely testing. Separate failure discovery from estimating its frequency, test-induced changes from prior material exposure, and human skill trajectories from broader adoption effects.

categories.label: Validity
categories.assessment: These ask what scores, judges and combined evidence warrant. Model confidence calibration concerns an evaluated system’s signals. Statistical uncertainty concerns the estimates produced by the evaluation. Formal assurance, local transfer and method complementarity need the boundary checks below.

categories.label: Deployment
categories.assessment: These use evaluation findings to forecast, report, monitor or estimate effects in practice. Separate fixed-system transfer, performance forecasts for changing systems and future evaluation requirements. Causal impacts of actual AI adoption fall within Definition 3.1.

categories.label: Lifecycle
categories.assessment: These follow evaluated objects, procedures and evidence through versions, access, exposure, replication and reporting choices. Training records belong here when the evaluation claim depends on them. Audit records are distinct from enforceable rights to inspect them.

categories.label: Institutions
categories.assessment: These concern rules, rights, incentives, standards and assigned responsibilities for evaluation. Keep resources and expertise distinct from freedom to set scope and publish. Focus post-deployment duties on obtaining, evaluating and acting on evidence.

categories.label: Purpose
categories.assessment: These concern whose goals, values and priorities drive evaluation. Distinguish deciding what and whose outcomes matter from estimating the outcomes, and selecting the priorities from tracing how agreed priorities are implemented.

findings.observation: Both descriptions introduce formal checks of parts of an AI decision process and ask what those checks support about the whole system. Their current difference is too implicit.
findings.distinction: Incomplete-observation assurance asks what passing tests or non-detection warrant. Compositional formal assurance asks whether proofs for particular components hold for the complete decision process under stated assumptions.

options.title: How much assurance can incomplete tests support?
options.description: When a test does not detect a failure, what conditions and outcomes can that evidence cover? State the untested conditions, assumptions and uncertainty relevant to use.
options.reason: Removing the formal-proof strand changes the candidate’s scope.

options.title: Combining formal guarantees for AI decisions
options.description: Which guarantees for components apply to the whole AI decision process? Check how learned components and changing conditions affect the guarantees.
options.reason: Making composition the primary research obstacle changes what is assessed.
The frozen version already focuses on what non-detection and incomplete tests can establish. Compare it alongside the formal-guarantee candidate with its existing scores and coverage.

findings.observation: C.V7 asks whether judges and entire evaluation methods share errors. G.V.PORTFOLIO also asks about shared assumptions and blind spots across tests.
findings.distinction: Validate one judge or one instrument against independent evidence. Then ask separately whether a second validated method adds evidence and which joint blind spots remain.

options.title: Validating individual judges and evaluation methods
options.description: Judges and tests can share errors with the system they assess. Compare each method against evidence gathered independently and identify where its conclusions fail.
options.reason: If this wording limits the candidate to single-method validation, reassess previously credited cross-method scope.
Retain the current focus on incremental evidence and joint blind spots, with an explicit cross-reference to individual-method validation. Adding that note alone leaves the research task unchanged.

findings.observation: C.V1a asks which claims hold across people or settings. G.V.LOCAL gives language and community transfer a dedicated entry. The K=35 numerical optimum retains the narrower entry and drops the general one.
findings.distinction: Interpreting a score in its original setting and checking that its interpretation survives adaptation are different claims. Transfer can be presented as a specific challenge under broad construct validity if manuscript space is limited.

options.reason: Compare the fixed K=35 portfolio with C.V1a required. Its existing wording and scores can be used unchanged. A constrained optimum was computed for review.
If folded into a new general validity version, retain changed task meaning, reference answers and local expectations as explicit examples and recode what the merged version covers.

findings.observation: C.D5 is rated Q1=3 and Q2=2. Its present wording can read as forecasting work requirements generally. The manuscript’s scope needs a clear connection to planning evaluation evidence.
findings.distinction: C.D2a forecasts behaviour of a changing system. C.T.TIMELY develops and maintains instruments. C.D5 needs to assess whether evidence can predict gaps in instruments for future workflows.

options.title: Predicting when evaluations will miss workflow needs
options.description: Which evaluation results and field observations can forecast the abilities a new workflow will require? Backtest whether those forecasts identify important abilities missing from current tests early enough to guide evaluation design.
options.reason: The narrower, testable claim should be reviewed against direct evidence about forecasting evaluation requirements and the intended planning decision.

findings.observation: C.T.RARE has low confidence and Q2=2. Its description already distinguishes discovering failures from estimating their frequency. That is a defensible Techniques boundary, but existing stress tests are partial approaches.
findings.distinction: Finding severe failures and near misses under an observation budget, estimating rates and making assurance claims from non-detection can succeed or fail independently.

options.reason: Compare current scenario selection and stress-testing research. Record which failure modes, conditions and resource budgets remain poorly covered. Retain as provisional until the residual obstacle and its source are clear.

If rare-failure discovery is moved under elicitation to fit the manuscript, retain the test-budget and near-miss discovery problem as a specific challenge. A merged general wording requires new scores and coverage.

findings.observation: N.P2.horizons has low confidence. Its first question sets the ethical scope of evaluation, while its question about proxy accuracy moves towards Validity. Estimating long-run effects also overlaps with C.D3a.
findings.distinction: Purpose sets whose effects and which time horizon count. Deployment estimates what adoption changes. Validity checks whether proxies support those claims.

options.title: Choosing which delayed effects evaluations count
options.description: Which groups and future periods should an AI evaluation represent, including impacts on non-users and shared resources? Explain who sets that boundary and how different choices change what the evaluation counts.
options.reason: This recasts the question as a choice about evaluation scope. Review the relevant stakeholder decisions and literature on existing horizon and externality approaches.
For a compact version, test a merger that explicitly preserves delayed effects and affected non-users alongside value conflicts. Treat it as a new candidate with a documented research boundary.

findings.observation: M.P.PRIORITIES is Q2=2. It is distinct from inviting participation or resolving value disagreement because it starts after agreement and asks whether the evaluation implements it. Evidence of how often and where this fails is limited.
findings.distinction: R.P1 covers whose priorities enter the agenda. N.P2.values covers disagreement about outcomes. M.P.PRIORITIES follows an agreed priority into an actual claim, measure and report.

options.title: Tracing agreed priorities into evaluations
options.description: When people agree what an AI evaluation should address, can they trace their priorities through the claims, measures and reports? Identify departures from agreed aims and make the reasons visible.
options.reason: The wording preserves the existing traceability task and affected groups.
Look for studies of whether evaluation claims, metrics and reports implement stated stakeholder commitments. Record the residual audit problem and where present tools already solve it.

findings.observation: The descriptions all mention resources or comparison conditions. The new resource item is most useful when it asks which cross-system conclusions hold under comparable budgets, including what is recorded about training and use.
findings.distinction: C.T.BASELINE chooses the best feasible alternative workflow. R.T2 identifies which causes explain a result. G.T.RESOURCES standardises resource accounting and comparisons.

options.reason: Name training, inference, tools and human support as separate inputs. Explain that matched comparisons should state the budget that matters for the use decision. Keep the current scope and tags only if all these facets remain.
If the scope is narrowed to test-time compute, re-rate the question and remove any unsupported training or human-resource coverage. Verify what existing resource-reporting approaches already cover.

findings.observation: The two selected interaction entries focus on different recurring failures. Compressing them into the existing umbrella changes the expanded model’s coverage, even if it saves a manuscript slot.
findings.distinction: M.T.SOCIAL concerns transfer to unfamiliar partners and group behaviour. M.T.HUMAN measures learning, reliance and skill over repeated use. C.D3a studies effects of adoption compared with feasible alternatives.

options.reason: Compare the existing umbrella for the shorter manuscript version using its current ratings. Inspect which two narrower outcomes its actual description and coded tags can support.
If rewritten to cover both group transfer and human change explicitly, re-evaluate the combined research scope, added stakeholder coverage and conflicts with the two narrower versions.

findings.observation: Both the deployed-system synthesis and public indicators involve summarising test evidence. The existing deployment umbrella can save a slot by combining reporting and a retest trigger, with explicit editorial consequences.
findings.distinction: C.D4b integrates evidence about a particular deployed system. G.D.INDICATORS compares public summaries across tests, systems or time and separates capability from prevalence. C.D4c asks when observations should trigger another evaluation.

options.reason: Make the public cross-test or time comparison explicit and retain capability versus prevalence. Cross-reference the single-system synthesis.
Use the existing reporting-and-monitoring umbrella for a compact option and compare the concrete scope lost from the two separate headings. The archived K=45 option uses this umbrella.

findings.observation: Both R.L4 and N.I3.audit discuss access, legitimate restrictions and independent checking. Their different levers should be explicit to avoid duplicating the same proposed remedy.
findings.distinction: Lifecycle asks how much evidence or interaction is technically sufficient under confidentiality or privacy constraints. Institutions asks who can demand evidence or contest a claim and through which enforceable procedure. C.L.SELECTION asks whether records reveal selective reporting.

options.title: Sufficient evidence for independent verification
options.description: What records or interactions allow an independent reviewer to check an evaluation claim? Test how privacy, security and confidentiality safeguards change what the reviewer can verify.
options.reason: Retains the existing sufficiency and access trade-off. Keep legal entitlements and appeals under Institutions.
Make legal rights, review procedures and remedies the centre of the description. Preserve the existing constraints on access and independent challenge.

findings.observation: Both candidates discuss distorted performance under testing. Exposure during inference can be confused with recognizing that an evaluation is underway.
findings.distinction: Techniques isolates how the evaluation protocol or test awareness changes the behaviour observed. Lifecycle traces whether test items or relevant information became available before the scored response.

options.title: Tracing exposure to evaluation material
options.reason: Clarify that exposure can occur during training, tool use or inference, as long as it precedes the scored response. Keep the effect on claims and uncertainty about unavailable records.

findings.observation: N.P4.benchmarks can read as a broad question about the direction of AI development. N.P4.agenda fits the paper’s own purpose when tied specifically to AI evaluation research priorities.
findings.distinction: Purpose studies how evaluation choices and public benchmarks redirect what gets measured or prioritised. Institutions studies who sets or enforces incentive arrangements. Agenda allocation can remain a separate problem about scarce evaluation effort.

options.title: What public AI benchmarks lead developers to optimize
options.description: A public score can redirect what developers measure, improve and disclose. How can evaluators test whether those changes serve the benchmark’s stated purpose?
options.reason: This narrows a broad progress claim to testable consequences for evaluation purposes and evidence.
Specify AI evaluation questions throughout the description and preserve the current focus on systematic omissions across agenda versions.

findings.observation: C.F1a’s second sentence about evidence transferring from a component to a whole can look like a validity question. C.F4a is also broader than the specific strength of an available evaluation.
findings.distinction: Foundations defines what system and claim are in scope and which distinctions can in principle be observed. Techniques isolates component contributions. Validity assesses whether actual evidence warrants a particular interpretation.

options.reason: Keep the unit-of-analysis and claim-boundary language first, and add a secondary cross-link for component-to-system evidence. Retain both current research facets.
Keep observations, interventions and resources explicit so readers see the question concerns identification limits in principle.

findings.observation: “Unfaithful” in the heading can be unclear to readers outside evaluation methods. The description has a coherent problem about realistic, safely controlled tests.
findings.distinction: The topic concerns properties of the test environment and safeguards for participants, with consequences for the behaviour observed.

options.title: Making evaluation settings safe and realistic
options.reason: Retain the existing description, including that safeguards can change the behaviour a study is trying to observe.

To require a version, begin the exact search with that version selected, its coverage credited and its conflicting versions removed. To make a pair exclusive, add a symmetric conflict. These are separate tests for author review.

stressTests.interpretation: The exact constrained optimum keeps general claim validity for a cost of 0.025237 points. K=36 already contains C.V1a.

stressTests.change: Require C.V4a and C.V6 to be mutually exclusive.

stressTests.change: Require C.V7 and G.V.PORTFOLIO to be mutually exclusive.
stressTests.interpretation: The optimizer splits the judge and method question into prior alternatives and merges reporting and monitoring to keep the fixed size. Clarifying the existing descriptions may be preferable to declaring a hard conflict.
