C.F1a.title: Unclear boundaries of evaluated systems
C.F1a.description: A model, its tools and the people using it can jointly determine what happens. Evaluators need rules for deciding what belongs to the system a claim covers, and when evidence about one component applies to the whole.
research_targets: Define and test claims over explicit system boundaries
Establish when component-level evidence warrants a system-level claim within a specified system boundary

C.F2a.title: Unclear definitions of abilities and tendencies
C.F2a.description: A test score alone cannot tell us what an AI system can do or what it tends to do in practice. We need definitions that distinguish these properties and can be revised when new evidence about behaviour or its causes disagrees with them.
research_targets: Connect ability and tendency definitions to evidence across contexts

C.F3a.title: Scores lack a shared meaning across tests
C.F3a.description: A higher score may reflect a different test, population or difficulty rather than a more capable system. Evaluators need defensible scales for comparing results and describing how broadly abilities apply, including when systems exceed existing tests.
research_targets: Identify invariant scales and legitimate limits of comparisons
Separate breadth and difficulty from instrument-specific thresholds

C.F4a.title: Limits on what evaluation can establish
C.F4a.description: Some systems can look identical in every test evaluators can run while behaving differently elsewhere. We need to know which claims can be settled with the observations, interventions and resources available, and what extra evidence would change the answer.
research_targets: Map identifiability limits under stated access and resource conditions

R.T2.title: Weak experimental control and causal diagnosis
R.T2.description: The same outcome can arise from very different mechanisms. Evaluation needs controlled comparisons and interventions that separate model, scaffold, human and environmental contributions. The open problem is to obtain explanations useful for diagnosis while retaining realistic conditions and accounting for interactions between components.
research_targets: Separate causal contributions of models, scaffolds, humans and environments using evaluation interventions
Establish fair and realistic comparisons against feasible human and human–AI workflows

R.T5.title: Unsafe or unfaithful evaluation environments
R.T5.description: A test environment must reveal relevant behaviour while containing harm and protecting participants. Sandboxes, simulated users and human studies can alter the phenomenon they are meant to study. We need environments whose safety constraints, realism and remaining distortions are explicit and experimentally examinable.
research_targets: Determine which environment constraints preserve relevant behaviour while proportionately containing harm
Determine how to protect participants and annotators while maintaining credible behavioural evidence

C.T.BASELINE.title: Choosing fair and realistic human and human–AI baselines
C.T.BASELINE.description: What comparison workflow, participant experience, resource budget and prior access make human, AI and hybrid performance meaningfully comparable? The evaluation must distinguish an artificial control from the best feasible alternative available to the people making the decision.
research_targets: Establish fair and realistic comparisons against feasible human and human–AI workflows

C.T.ELICIT.title: Eliciting consequential behaviour under known conditions
C.T.ELICIT.description: How can evaluation procedures reveal consequential capabilities, tendencies and failures under a specified system configuration and resource budget? We need evidence that the evaluation gave the system a suitable opportunity to act and that the test conditions did not substitute a different capability for the one of interest.
research_targets: Design elicitation methods that separate behaviour revealed from assumptions about resources and opportunities
Identify how testing changes behaviour and bound that distortion in evaluation design
Design and compare tests for discovering meaningful rare failure modes under stated operating conditions

C.T.RARE.title: Discovering rare but consequential failures
C.T.RARE.description: How can evaluators choose scenarios, observation horizons and stress conditions that are informative about rare failure modes in a specified domain of use? Tests need to surface meaningful failures and near misses without confusing discovery coverage with estimates of how frequently the failures occur.
research_targets: Design and compare tests for discovering meaningful rare failure modes under stated operating conditions

C.T.REACTIVITY.title: Testing changes the behaviour it is meant to measure
C.T.REACTIVITY.description: How can evaluators tell when a system behaves differently because it is being tested, and design comparisons that estimate the resulting distortion? The challenge includes changes caused by the testing protocol itself as well as changes when a system recognises the evaluation context.
research_targets: Identify how testing changes behaviour and bound that distortion in evaluation design

C.T.TIMELY.title: Developing and maintaining tests in time for emerging capabilities
C.T.TIMELY.description: How can evaluators prepare, validate and refresh instruments in time to assess emerging capabilities under limited compute and expert time? Adaptive task selection and benchmark repair need to preserve coverage and meaningful discrimination as systems and uses change.
research_targets: Determine how to preserve test coverage, discrimination and verifiability within a fixed budget
Design, validate and maintain tests in time for emerging capability changes

C.V1a.title: Scores can support the wrong conclusions
C.V1a.description: An evaluation score can reflect shortcuts or features of the test instead of the ability or risk it is meant to measure. Evaluators need to show which conclusions a result supports, for which people or settings, and what evidence rules out other explanations.
research_targets: Test competing explanations and document evidence for interpretations

C.V3a.title: Overconfidence in rankings and risk estimates
C.V3a.description: Small or repeatedly selected samples can make model rankings unstable and rare failures hard to estimate. Evaluators need uncertainty estimates that reflect how tests were collected and show which conclusions hold across groups, including where the evidence is too sparse to tell.
stakeholders: Oversight bodies and people exposed to harms
research_targets: Calibrate uncertainty under dependence, selection and heterogeneity
Design and validate estimates for rare-event rates and uncertainty

C.V4a.title: Weak assurance about AI system behaviour
C.V4a.description: Passing tests does not establish that a failure is impossible. Formal checks may establish properties of parts of a decision process under stated assumptions. We need ways to assess what tests and proofs jointly establish and what uncertainty remains.
stakeholders: Deployers, oversight bodies and people exposed to harms
research_targets: Derive bounded assurance accounting for coverage and search limits
Compare formal guarantees with empirical checks of assumptions and scope

C.V6.title: Limited formal assurance for AI decisions
C.V6.description: Formal checks can establish some properties of a specified decision process, but an AI system may include learned components and changing surroundings. Which parts can be checked, how can we test the assumptions, and what conclusions apply to the complete system?
research_targets: Compare formal guarantees with empirical checks of assumptions and scope

C.V7.title: Unreliable judges and evaluation methods
C.V7.description: When tests and judges use similar models or data, they can agree while sharing the same errors. We need ways to check difficult answers against trustworthy standards and to test whether whole evaluation methods work, using evidence independent of the systems being evaluated.
stakeholders: Evaluators and users of evaluation results
research_targets: Develop and calibrate reference standards for hard-to-judge work
Test evaluator reliability with independent evidence and controls

R.D1.title: Weak prediction beyond tested conditions
R.D1.description: Evaluation is useful when it informs behaviour in conditions that were not directly tested. We need models of how results transfer across tasks, users, interfaces and operational settings. These predictions must identify their assumptions and failure conditions rather than treating a benchmark score as a universal deployment forecast.
research_targets: Validate transfer models against held-out operational conditions

C.D2a.title: Forecasts break when AI systems change
C.D2a.description: Tests of current systems give only partial evidence about later models or systems that learn during use. We need forecasts that state what changes they assume, how far ahead they apply, and how their uncertainty changes when the system evolves in other ways.
research_targets: Compare and calibrate forecasts across system changes

C.D3a.title: Unclear effects of adopting AI
C.D3a.description: Better task scores do not show what happens when people adopt an AI system. We need comparisons with realistic alternatives that estimate what adoption changes for users, workers and non-users, including who benefits or bears harms over time.
stakeholders: Workers, users, non-users and oversight bodies
research_targets: Identify adoption effects using credible comparisons and designs
Estimate effects across affected groups and time horizons

C.D4b.title: Fragmented evidence about deployed AI
C.D4b.description: Evidence about a system is spread across test reports, incident records and user observations. We need ways to combine these accounts so people can tell what they support, where they disagree, and what information is still missing for a decision.
research_targets: Combine tests and operational evidence without masking conflicts

C.D4c.title: Unclear when monitoring should trigger new tests
C.D4c.description: After deployment, unexpected incidents and shifts in behaviour may reveal that earlier tests missed important risks. We need monitoring that can notice new problems and evidence for deciding when to reopen or expand an evaluation.
research_targets: Test how monitoring identifies new failures and informs re-evaluation

C.D5.title: Limited anticipation of future capability needs
C.D5.description: New uses can require abilities that existing tests do not assess. We need ways to forecast which abilities future workflows will require and how far in advance those forecasts are reliable enough to guide evaluation planning.
research_targets: Backtest predictions of which capabilities future tasks will require

R.L3.title: Untraceable system and evidence changes
R.L3.description: A result applies to a particular system and procedure, yet both change over time. We need to trace versions, configurations, data and derived claims, and determine which evidence remains applicable after a change. Traceability must connect the evaluated object to the one actually used.
research_targets: Link a specific evaluation claim to its tested system, dependencies, data and configuration
Determine which evidence survives a specified configuration or procedure change and which needs retesting

R.L4.title: Inadequate access for independent verification
R.L4.description: Independent verification requires access appropriate to the claim, while unrestricted disclosure can compromise privacy, security and legitimate confidentiality. We need technical and procedural arrangements that expose sufficient evidence without creating unnecessary risks. The adequacy of access must itself be testable.
research_targets: Determine the minimum verification access required by different claim types
Assess how confidentiality and privacy protections change independent verification power

C.L.EXPOSURE.title: Establishing whether evaluation evidence is independent of prior exposure
C.L.EXPOSURE.description: How can evaluators detect exposure to test content during training, through tools or scaffolds, and during inference? They need to assess how exposure changes the interpretation of performance, including cases where the system’s training or retrieval history is only partly available.
research_targets: Detect and account for evaluation exposure across training and runtime channels

C.L.REPRODUCE.title: Reproducing evaluations and the training evidence they depend on
C.L.REPRODUCE.description: What records and tolerances let an independent team rerun inference and scoring, check whether an evaluation’s conclusions recur, and diagnose discrepancies? When a claim depends on how a model was trained, which training records or artifacts are also needed?
research_targets: Specify records and acceptable variation for reproducing a claim-bearing evaluation procedure
Identify when evaluation-relevant training histories and artifacts must be available to reconstruct evidence

C.L.SELECTION.title: Making selective evaluation and reporting auditable
C.L.SELECTION.description: How can evaluators account for the runs, prompts, benchmarks and analysis choices that produced a reported result? Preregistration, searchable evaluation records and clear explanations of exploratory changes should be assessed by whether they make selective evidence visible.
research_targets: Audit the sampling, search and reporting choices that shaped the retained evaluation record

R.I1.title: Unclear rules connecting evidence to action
R.I1.description: Evidence does not determine action without rules about acceptable uncertainty, stakes and available alternatives. Institutions need defensible ways to connect findings and missing evidence to approval, restrictions, remediation or withdrawal. These rules must remain meaningful as systems and evaluation methods improve.
research_targets: Test evidence thresholds against different stakes, uncertainty and available actions
Compare reversible decision rules when material evidence is unavailable

N.I2.capacity.title: Unequal capacity to evaluate AI independently
N.I2.capacity.description: Independent evaluations require expertise, stable resources and facilities. Which arrangements let less-resourced groups run consequential evaluations and sustain their capacity as the systems and methods change?
research_targets: Test ways of broadening independent evaluation capability across institutions and regions

N.I2.independence.title: Protecting the independence of AI evaluators
N.I2.independence.description: Evaluators need discretion to set the scope, conduct tests and publish material findings when evaluated providers supply resources or models. Which funding and governance arrangements preserve that discretion across the evaluation process?
research_targets: Compare governance arrangements for independent agenda-setting and publication

N.I3.audit.title: Enforcing rights to audit and challenge evaluations
N.I3.audit.description: An independent auditor or affected group may need evidence that the evaluated provider controls. Which rights and review procedures make consequential claims auditable and contestable while respecting legitimate access restrictions?
research_targets: Compare enforceable audit access and challenge mechanisms against actual evidence needs

N.I3.duties.title: Assigning responsibility for evaluation after deployment
N.I3.duties.description: Different organizations may control the model, deployment, logs and ability to intervene. How should evaluation, incident reporting and response duties be allocated so emerging problems are detected and acted on?
research_targets: Evaluate duty allocation when several actors control the deployed system and its evidence

N.I4.incentives.title: Aligning incentives for informative AI evaluation
N.I4.incentives.description: Organizations can benefit from favorable tests or leave monitoring costs to others. Which incentives and cost-sharing arrangements lead to useful tests, candid reporting and sustained monitoring?
research_targets: Compare coordination and cost-sharing designs for monitoring transparency
Test whether evaluation incentives reduce selective or low-information testing

R.P1.title: Missing voices in evaluation agendas
R.P1.description: Evaluation agendas can overlook those affected by AI who do not build or directly use it. We need ways for different forms of knowledge and underrepresented perspectives to influence question selection, concepts and interpretation. Participation must change consequential choices and remain open to disagreement.
research_targets: Test which forms of participation materially change agenda or metric decisions
Identify overlooked questions by comparing stakeholder priorities with evaluator agendas

R.P3.title: Misallocated evaluation effort
R.P3.description: No agenda can investigate every important question. We need principled ways to allocate effort across immediate harms, future risks, benefits and neglected evidence gaps. Priorities should consider decision value, irreversibility and uncertainty, while resisting the tendency to equate convenient tests or abundant publications with importance.
research_targets: Compare prioritization rules using decision value, irreversibility, uncertainty and resource constraints

N.P2.horizons.title: Accounting for delayed and indirect evaluation outcomes
N.P2.horizons.description: Short evaluation windows can leave effects on non-users, future users and resource use outside the decision. Which indirect and delayed outcomes should be included, and when do practical proxies misrepresent them?
research_targets: Compare which indirect and delayed outcomes enter evaluation boundaries and how proxies affect decisions

N.P2.values.title: Making conflicting values visible in evaluation
N.P2.values.description: People can disagree about what an AI system should achieve, whose outcomes should count, and which trade-offs are acceptable. How can evaluations reflect those differences, including effects on autonomy, without hiding them in one summary score?
research_targets: Compare representations of conflicting values without hiding distributional trade-offs
Test agency-sensitive criteria against throughput-only indicators

N.P4.agenda.title: Detecting blind spots in AI-assisted evaluation agendas
N.P4.agenda.description: AI can help discover, phrase and prioritize evaluation questions, changing which concerns get attention. How can people detect systematic omissions across agenda revisions and decide when to revise the selection process?
research_targets: Detect systematic omissions from AI-assisted selection over successive agenda cycles

N.P4.benchmarks.title: Benchmark incentives and the direction of AI development
N.P4.benchmarks.description: Published benchmarks can direct effort towards measured targets and away from other capabilities or impacts. How can evaluators identify such shifts and judge whether they represent useful progress?
research_targets: Measure causal changes in development priorities after evaluative signals are introduced

G.V.CALIBRATION.title: Testing whether AI confidence is trustworthy
G.V.CALIBRATION.description: An AI system may express confidence or defer to a person without having a well-defined probability of being correct. How can evaluators check whether these signals track reliability for different tasks and populations, including after conditions change?
research_targets: Validate output confidence and abstention across task types, levels of granularity and shifts

G.T.RESOURCES.title: Comparing performance under unequal resource use
G.T.RESOURCES.description: Models can obtain similar scores using different amounts of training, inference, tools and human support. How should evaluations record these inputs and compare performance under comparable constraints, so apparent gains can be distinguished from additional resource use?
research_targets: Validate resource boundaries, reporting and performance–cost comparisons for different evaluation configurations

G.V.LOCAL.title: Validating evaluations across languages and communities
G.V.LOCAL.description: A test that works in one language or community can change meaning when it is translated or reused. What evidence can distinguish a real performance gap from a shift in the task, reference answers or local expectations, and when is a new test needed?
research_targets: Validate criteria for choosing translation, cultural adaptation, or local reconstruction of an evaluation
Test competing explanations and document evidence for interpretations

G.D.INDICATORS.title: Making AI evaluation indicators useful to the public
G.D.INDICATORS.description: Public indicators need to make results from many tests understandable while retaining what was tested, how widely a capability is used, and where the evidence is weak. Which summaries help non-specialists interpret changes and use the evidence in decisions?
research_targets: Test public summaries of AI evaluation for comprehension, comparability and decision usefulness
Combine tests and operational evidence without masking conflicts

G.I.STANDARDS.title: Keeping shared evaluation standards current
G.I.STANDARDS.description: Evaluation standards must evolve as systems and methods change, while institutions still need to compare results obtained under earlier rules. Who should revise shared standards, and what evidence and transition procedures make changes timely and interpretable?
research_targets: Compare institutional revision and transition mechanisms for shared evaluation standards

G.V.PORTFOLIO.title: Combining tests without repeating their blind spots
G.V.PORTFOLIO.description: An evaluation may combine several tests, but they can rely on the same assumptions or miss the same behaviours. How can evaluators decide whether a new method adds independent evidence and identify which uncertainties still limit the combined claim?
research_targets: Test method complementarity and shared blind spots when combining evaluation evidence

M.T.SOCIAL.title: Tests miss behaviour with unfamiliar AI partners
M.T.SOCIAL.description: Agents may cooperate well with familiar partners and fail when the mix changes. We need tests across partner populations and roles that reveal which behaviours transfer, which depend on shared conventions, and which failures only appear at the group level.
research_targets: Measure behaviours that emerge from interaction among humans and AI systems or among AI systems
Test population-dependent collective behaviour with held-out partners and roles

M.T.HUMAN.title: Tests miss how human–AI teams change
M.T.HUMAN.description: AI assistance can improve a team’s immediate output while changing how people understand a task, rely on advice or develop skills. Evaluations need to observe people and AI working together over time and check whether simulated users capture the responses that matter.
stakeholders: Users and workers in AI-assisted teams
research_targets: Measure behaviours that emerge from interaction among humans and AI systems or among AI systems
Design longitudinal tests for behaviour that changes with interaction history, adaptation or learning
Design repeated human–AI studies that distinguish performance from changes in human understanding and reliance

M.P.PRIORITIES.title: Agreed priorities get lost in evaluation practice
M.P.PRIORITIES.description: People can agree on what matters and still receive tests or reports that answer different questions. We need ways to check whether priorities survive the choice of claims, measures and reported results, and to make departures visible to those affected.
research_targets: Audit whether agreed priorities are retained across claims, measures and reported outcomes

R.F1.title: Unclear objects and boundaries of evaluation
R.F1.description: An evaluation must specify what system, population and context its claims concern. Models, tools, memories, people and institutions can jointly determine behaviour. We lack a principled account of when these components form the relevant evaluation object and which changes create a different object.
research_targets: Define and test claims over explicit system boundaries
Establish when component-level evidence warrants a system-level claim within a specified system boundary

R.F2.title: Weak theories of capabilities and propensities
R.F2.description: What a system can do differs from what it tends to do. Both require concepts that survive beyond one benchmark and distinguish abilities, preferences and context. The open problem is to connect explicit definitions, empirical structure and explanatory models without treating convenient scores as the properties themselves.
research_targets: Connect ability and tendency definitions to evidence across contexts

R.F3.title: Incommensurable scales and generality claims
R.F3.description: Evaluation scores often lack a shared meaning across tests, populations and time. A higher percentage need not represent the same improvement everywhere. We need defensible scales for breadth, difficulty and behavioural tendencies, including extreme capability, without assuming that all valued properties fit one number.
research_targets: Identify invariant scales and legitimate limits of comparisons
Separate breadth and difficulty from instrument-specific thresholds

R.F4.title: Unknown limits of behavioural evaluability
R.F4.description: Some behavioural properties cannot be distinguished using the observations and interventions an evaluator can obtain. We need to map these limits under explicit assumptions about access, resources and strategic behaviour. The challenge is to identify when improved instruments could resolve uncertainty, when additional kinds of evidence are needed, and when a claim must remain conditional.
research_targets: Map identifiability limits under stated access and resource conditions

R.T1.title: Inadequate elicitation of consequential behaviour
R.T1.description: Observed performance depends on how a system is prompted, assisted and challenged. Evaluation methods must expose consequential abilities and tendencies under specified resources, including behaviour hidden by training or strategic underperformance. The challenge is to elicit informative behaviour without silently changing what capability is being tested.
research_targets: Design elicitation methods that separate behaviour revealed from assumptions about resources and opportunities
Identify how testing changes behaviour and bound that distortion in evaluation design
Design and compare tests for discovering meaningful rare failure modes under stated operating conditions

R.T3.title: Tests miss interactions and evolving trajectories
R.T3.description: Consequential behaviour can emerge only through repeated interaction, collective action or learning. Instruments must study human–AI groups, agent populations and changing instances over meaningful horizons. Isolated task success is insufficient to reveal accumulated harm, coordination, collusion or the conditions under which control is lost.
research_targets: Measure behaviours that emerge from interaction among humans and AI systems or among AI systems
Design longitudinal tests for behaviour that changes with interaction history, adaptation or learning

R.T4.title: Testing cannot keep pace with change
R.T4.description: Evaluation competes with rapid changes in systems and tasks under limited expertise, time and compute. We need adaptive instruments that remain informative as tests saturate or become obsolete. Efficiency must preserve important coverage and verifiability rather than reward only the behaviours that are easiest to test.
research_targets: Determine how to preserve test coverage, discrimination and verifiability within a fixed budget
Design, validate and maintain tests in time for emerging capability changes

C.T.ATTRIB.title: Attributing evaluation outcomes to the right causes
C.T.ATTRIB.description: How can evaluators distinguish the contributions of the model, tools, scaffold, people and environment to the same observed outcome? Controlled interventions should provide diagnostic evidence while preserving the conditions and interactions that matter for the claim.
research_targets: Separate causal contributions of models, scaffolds, humans and environments using evaluation interventions
Establish fair and realistic comparisons against feasible human and human–AI workflows

C.T.ENVIRONMENT.title: Designing safe and realistic evaluation environments
C.T.ENVIRONMENT.description: How can evaluators preserve the conditions needed to observe relevant behaviour while limiting risk to participants, annotators and people outside the study? The evaluation should state which safeguards restrict behaviour and how those restrictions affect what the test can reveal.
research_targets: Determine which environment constraints preserve relevant behaviour while proportionately containing harm
Determine how to protect participants and annotators while maintaining credible behavioural evidence

C.T.INTERACTION.title: Testing interaction and behaviour over time
C.T.INTERACTION.description: How can evaluations observe behaviour that emerges only as AI systems interact with people or other systems, or as their behaviour changes with experience? Relevant partners, interaction histories and observation horizons must be chosen to reveal joint performance and cumulative failures.
research_targets: Measure behaviours that emerge from interaction among humans and AI systems or among AI systems
Design longitudinal tests for behaviour that changes with interaction history, adaptation or learning

R.V1.title: Unsupported interpretations of evaluation results
R.V1.description: A score supports a claim only through assumptions about what was measured and why the observations bear on it. We need evidence that distinguishes intended properties from shortcuts and alternative explanations. Interpretations must be reconsidered when the population, construct or intended use changes.
research_targets: Test competing explanations and document evidence for interpretations

R.V2.title: Unreliable grading and reference standards
R.V2.description: Judging a response can be harder than producing it. Human raters, model judges and automatic checks may share errors or reward the wrong properties. We need trustworthy reference standards and ways to bound disagreement and manipulation, especially for open-ended outputs and work exceeding individual human expertise.
research_targets: Develop and calibrate reference standards for hard-to-judge work

R.V3.title: Uncalibrated uncertainty and system comparisons
R.V3.description: Finite and adaptively selected observations can give unstable comparisons and overconfident risk estimates. We need uncertainty estimates that account for sampling, dependencies, repeated trials, selective reporting and heterogeneous populations. Reliable average performance must not conceal severe failures or unjustified certainty about particular groups.
stakeholders: Oversight bodies and people exposed to harms
research_targets: Calibrate uncertainty under dependence, selection and heterogeneity
Design and validate estimates for rare-event rates and uncertainty

R.V4.title: Weak evidence for absence and assurance
R.V4.description: Not observing a failure or ability does not establish its absence. We need explicit assumptions linking search effort, coverage and adversarial behaviour to the assurance a decision requires. The central challenge is to state meaningful bounds and residual uncertainty when complete testing is impossible.
stakeholders: Deployers, oversight bodies and people exposed to harms
research_targets: Derive bounded assurance accounting for coverage and search limits

R.V5.title: Unvalidated evaluators and evaluation methods
R.V5.description: Evaluation methods themselves need testing. Synthetic populations, model-generated tasks, interpretability tools and automated oversight can fail together with the systems they assess. We need independent calibration and evidence about where a method works, including safeguards against circular validation as AI increasingly produces its own tests.
stakeholders: Evaluators and users of evaluation results
research_targets: Test evaluator reliability with independent evidence and controls

R.D2.title: Unreliable forecasts of evolving systems
R.D2.description: Future systems and continually changing instances may behave differently from what current tests suggest. We need forecasts conditional on time, learning, resources and interaction, with calibrated uncertainty. Forecasting a particular trajectory must be distinguished from merely showing that some future behaviour is reachable.
research_targets: Compare and calibrate forecasts across system changes

R.D3.title: Unmeasured causal and distributional impacts
R.D3.description: What AI can do does not establish what adopting it causes. We need credible comparisons with alternatives to estimate effects on users, workers, non-users and institutions. The challenge includes delayed outcomes, unequal benefits and harms, and changes in behaviour caused by the adoption itself.
stakeholders: Workers, users, non-users and oversight bodies
research_targets: Identify adoption effects using credible comparisons and designs
Estimate effects across affected groups and time horizons

R.D4.title: Fragmented evidence for use and monitoring
R.D4.description: Decision makers must combine tests, limitations, incidents and observations from use. These sources are often incomplete, incompatible or too difficult to interpret. We need faithful synthesis and feedback mechanisms that reveal new problems, trigger appropriate re-evaluation and retain uncertainty throughout a system’s use.
research_targets: Combine tests and operational evidence without masking conflicts
Test how monitoring identifies new failures and informs re-evaluation

C.D4a.title: Disconnected evaluation and monitoring evidence
C.D4a.description: Test reports, limits, incidents and observations from real use are often hard to combine. We need ways to show what the evidence supports, preserve disagreement and uncertainty, and use new observations to decide when to test a deployed system again.
research_targets: Combine tests and operational evidence without masking conflicts
Test how monitoring identifies new failures and informs re-evaluation

R.L1.title: Compromised integrity of evaluation evidence
R.L1.description: Evidence can be distorted by leaked tests, selective reporting and optimisation against known evaluations. We need ways to establish how evidence was produced and what information influenced the system. Integrity must remain checkable even when training data and evaluation searches are not publicly available.
research_targets: Detect and account for evaluation exposure across training and runtime channels
Audit the sampling, search and reporting choices that shaped the retained evaluation record

R.L2.title: Unreproducible evaluation processes
R.L2.description: Others must be able to reconstruct how a result was obtained and test whether it persists. Dynamic services, undocumented choices and expert-dependent procedures make this difficult. We need reproducibility standards appropriate to different evaluation objects, including transparent records of exploration and unavoidable variation.
research_targets: Specify records and acceptable variation for reproducing a claim-bearing evaluation procedure

C.L.LINEAGE.title: Tracing evaluated systems and when evidence applies
C.L.LINEAGE.description: How can evaluators and auditors link a claim to the versions of the model, tools, data and procedure that produced it? When the deployed configuration or the test changes, they need to establish which earlier claims can still be supported and which need fresh evidence.
research_targets: Link a specific evaluation claim to its tested system, dependencies, data and configuration
Determine which evidence survives a specified configuration or procedure change and which needs retesting

R.I2.title: Dependent evaluators and unequal evaluation capacity
R.I2.description: An evaluation ecosystem needs people able to ask consequential questions and publish credible findings independently. Funding, access, infrastructure and expertise can concentrate control over what is evaluated. We need arrangements that sustain competence, diverse knowledge and independence throughout question selection, execution and interpretation.
research_targets: Compare governance arrangements for independent agenda-setting and publication
Test ways of broadening independent evaluation capability across institutions and regions

R.I3.title: Unenforceable duties and rights of challenge
R.I3.description: Useful evidence requires institutions able to obtain it, assign responsibility and respond to challenge. Distributed supply chains can leave monitoring, disclosure and remedy without an accountable owner. We need enforceable duties and accessible ways for affected people and independent evaluators to question consequential claims.
research_targets: Compare enforceable audit access and challenge mechanisms against actual evidence needs
Evaluate duty allocation when several actors control the deployed system and its evidence

R.I4.title: Misaligned incentives and fragmented evaluation governance
R.I4.description: Actors may benefit from weak tests, favourable reporting or leaving costly monitoring to others. Cross-organisational and international dependencies make isolated improvements insufficient. We need institutions that reward informative evaluation, coordinate shared responsibilities and can themselves be assessed for whether they improve outcomes.
research_targets: Compare coordination and cost-sharing designs for monitoring transparency
Test whether evaluation incentives reduce selective or low-information testing

R.P2.title: Unresolved conflicts over valued outcomes
R.P2.description: Stakeholders can disagree about which outcomes matter and how benefits, harms and autonomy should be compared. Evaluation needs explicit, revisable accounts of these choices and their distribution across people and time. A single aggregate measure must not conceal value conflict or replace political judgment.
research_targets: Compare representations of conflicting values without hiding distributional trade-offs
Test agency-sensitive criteria against throughput-only indicators

R.P4.title: Unexamined effects of evaluation on progress
R.P4.description: Evaluations change the systems, incentives and research agendas they observe. Their metrics can improve performance, distort priorities or delegate consequential choices to the AI being assessed. We need to examine these effects, including evaluation’s own costs, and keep the direction of progress open to accountable human revision.
research_targets: Measure causal changes in development priorities after evaluative signals are introduced
Detect systematic omissions from AI-assisted selection over successive agenda cycles

N.P4.feedback.title: How evaluations reshape development and research priorities
N.P4.feedback.description: Benchmarks influence what developers optimize, while AI-assisted agenda setting can influence what evaluators choose to study. How can we detect when those feedback effects promote useful progress or systematically obscure questions that matter?
research_targets: Measure causal changes in development priorities after evaluative signals are introduced
Detect systematic omissions from AI-assisted selection over successive agenda cycles

manuscript_review.summary: The two manuscript versions list the same 37 problem headings. The paper describes the set as about 35 problems. Personalization moved to §4.2.5 in the 10 November draft, shifting the subsection numbers for T.5, T.6a and T.6b. The screening crosswalk uses the 6 November manuscript.
manuscript_review.recheck: Read the changed bodies before claiming coverage of the newer draft. Start with personalization as an evaluation of user-conditioned behaviour and human–AI groups as an evaluation of heterogeneous participant effects. The expanded validity, deployment, lifecycle and institutional discussions also need current-draft review.
manuscript_review.appendix_a: The same ten-topic model-generated list appears in both drafts as an illustration of possible AI influence on agenda setting. The screening archive identifies the earlier manuscript, Programme and documented source evidence as its inputs.
manuscript_review.section_six: Section 6 remains a placeholder for closing priorities and next steps in the 10 November draft.

generation_upstream.title: From source records to the first candidate pool
generation_upstream.summary: The November 7 ranking selects one formulation per eligible research target. The November 8 synthesis uses those representatives to check coverage of 30 top-down general-problem proposals. A later freeze retains the 30 proposals and adds 37 editorial alternatives for portfolio selection.

stages.title: Record source evidence and check scope
inputs: 26 entries in the original Table 2 catalog and two supplementary sources
stages.method: Preserve each record’s identifier, source locator, version, verification status and extraction type. Record whether it is directly or indirectly relevant to evaluation or outside the scope. Distinguish explicit source questions, paraphrases, reformulated research directions and editorial inferences.
outputs: 1,095 records after adding 281, including 73 from the two supplementary sources
1,091 separate source score rows and four aliases without a separate score
stages.limits: The registry covers the inspected sources within documented extraction boundaries. The ledger records AI-assisted source checks and pending independent human verification.

stages.title: Rank sources and choose manuscript formulation representatives
inputs: 438 tracked manuscript formulations and 87 fixed interchangeable-target relations
stages.method: Apply the frozen rubric to the source and manuscript score tables separately. Group faithful rewrites by the same central research target. Keep narrower facets, umbrella syntheses and derivations as linked relationships. Choose the highest-ranked eligible manuscript-ready formulation in each fixed family.
outputs: 801 eligible source rows with recorded dispositions
stages.limits: The historical ledger provisionally reuses source scores when the manuscript keeps the wording, and records contextual re-ratings separately. Family membership and score judgments are inputs to the replay.

stages.title: Build and audit 30 general-problem proposals
inputs: Seven top-down evaluation functions, stakeholder decision requirements and 37 earlier manuscript entries
stages.method: Describe recurring obstacles to each evaluation function. Retain distinct obstacles when solving one can leave the other unresolved. Map each active formulation to a primary general problem and optional secondary links, then choose examples from the recorded direct-primary mappings.
outputs: 30 general-problem proposals and a 327-row coverage map
273 direct mappings, 49 needing an evaluation-focused rewrite and five ambiguous mappings
60 illustrative questions, including 57 source-grounded formulations and three separately supplied editorial syntheses
stages.limits: Topic boundaries, source mappings and example seeds are editorial judgments. This development-corpus audit tests the proposed structure within the recorded material.

stages.title: Freeze 67 candidate versions for portfolio selection
inputs: 30 prior general-problem proposals, 60 illustrative questions and earlier manuscript lineage
Expert feedback and separately documented wording and grouping alternatives
stages.method: Keep the exact English headings and descriptions of all 30 proposals. Add 37 revisions, splits, merges and gap variants. Record new Q1–Q5 judgments, source evidence, coverage tags and version conflicts for the candidate-level optimization.
outputs: Candidate source trails combining inherited examples, manuscript context and additional expert inputs
stages.limits: The 37 new versions and the 37 earlier manuscript entries are different inventories. The transition depends on editorial drafting and recoding, with a partly unnormalised extraction-to-candidate trail.

gateOrder: Hold if any score is missing, fractional or outside 0–3.
Exclude as written if any of G, I, U or T is zero.
Merge or consolidate if D is below 2.
Keep provisionally if all five scores are at least 2.
Develop if any of I, U or T is below 2.
Otherwise revise the general relevance or framing.
ranking.eligibility: A provisional keep also requires direct or documented indirect scope and the recorded evidence-eligibility flag. Family choice additionally requires manuscript readiness.
ranking.familyRule: Choose the first eligible manuscript-ready wording in each fixed interchangeable-target family. Rank representatives by the same sort key. All active families remain available without a fixed quota.
ranking.openness: U=2 was provisional and applies to all 801 eligible source rows and all 327 active representatives in this snapshot.

examples.method: Among direct-primary formulations, prefer the recorded editorial seed order, then a Table 2 representative, then higher earlier total and ascending formulation ID. Take the first and prefer a second with an additional source ID. Fill from the same order if necessary.
examples.limits: These examples illustrate a general problem. An additional source ID indicates recorded diversity. The three editorial syntheses retain links to supporting parents and have no new upstream score.

handoffs.trace: Stable source IDs, wording history and relation records link extractions to manuscript formulations or retained facets. Each of the 801 eligible source rows has a documented disposition.
handoffs.limit: The source and manuscript score tables serve different editorial contexts. Unchanged wording may carry forward a provisional source score.

handoffs.trace: The archived ranking IDs exactly match the 327 development-bank records. A saved primary and secondary map connects them to the proposals, and the example rule runs on the fixed map.
handoffs.limit: Stakeholder analysis, topic boundaries, semantic mappings and example seed priorities are supplied judgments. The ranking provides audit material for the 30 proposals.

handoffs.trace: The freeze preserves all 30 English title and description strings and records 37 additional versions. The candidate source trail contains both structured example references and narrative source annotations.
handoffs.limit: This handoff requires editorial generation, scope assessment and a new rubric. A complete machine-readable join from every new version to extraction IDs remains to be documented.

replay.scope: The package replays source ranking, fixed family choice, the exact 327-ID handoff and selection of the 57 source-grounded examples. It checks the three editorial example positions. All record identifiers are opaque aliases and original source text is absent.

limits: The upstream GIUTD rubric uses 0–3 and ranks specific formulations. The later Q1–Q5 rubric uses 0–4 and evaluates general-problem versions. Both sets of ratings remain tied to their own context.
The checks reproduce the consequences of frozen choices. Source extraction, source verification, current openness, taxonomy construction and author decisions remain separate review tasks.
Distinct source records can belong to a shared evidence family. Treat source roles and scholarly independence separately.

openness_review.title: Targeted evidence review of four screening candidates
openness_review.scope: Compare each candidate with selected public source passages and bounded empirical studies. Separate support for the framing or an existing method from evidence about the residual research claim.
openness_review.limits: This targeted review does not establish field-wide openness, coverage, or novelty. Additional sources are contextual comparisons added after the frozen run. Proposed text is for review. The screening ratings and membership were not revised.

items.disposition: Keep provisional as a Techniques question on failure discovery
items.recorded_source_correction: Anwar et al. motivate informative testing under resource constraints. The source question is about capability evaluation and should be labeled a methodological precedent for the budget dimension.

sources.title: Anwar et al., Foundational Challenges in Assuring Alignment and Safety of Large Language Models
sources.locator: arXiv v2, §2.2.4, author question 18, printed p. 22
sources.establishes: The authors pose a resource-constrained capability-evaluation design question, including informative and adaptive tests.
sources.boundary: The passage poses a question. It provides no test of rare-event coverage or of near-miss indicators.

sources.title: Anthropic, Bloom: an open source tool for automated behavioral evaluations
sources.locator: Sections on interpreting metrics and model choice in ideation and rollout
sources.establishes: Generated scenario suites can elicit specified behaviors. In the reported experiments, evaluator configuration influenced the scenario distribution and observed elicitation rates.
sources.boundary: Bloom describes limited ground truth on actual behavior prevalence. The suite’s elicitation rates are conditional on its tests and are insufficient to infer deployment frequency.

sources.title: Koren et al., Adaptive Stress Testing for Autonomous Vehicles
sources.establishes: Simulation-guided search found collision scenarios for a defined crosswalk case. One reported search configuration used fewer simulator calls and found higher-likelihood scenarios under the simulator model.
sources.boundary: The finding is conditional on the simulator and its assumptions. It supplies a comparison method for that setting and limited evidence about transfer.

items.unverified_claim: The inspected sources do not show which scenario and observation-horizon choices improve discovery of distinct, independently confirmed failure modes and useful near misses at a fixed budget across specified conditions of use.
items.proposed_title: Finding rare failures under a test budget
items.proposed_question: For a specified setting and test budget, which scenarios and observation horizons reveal distinct severe failures or meaningful near misses? Report discovery coverage separately from deployment-frequency estimates.
items.evidence_check: Compare representative and stress-focused suites on equal budgets in one domain with predeclared failure families and independently reviewed near misses. State the target conditions and which parts of the domain remain untested.

items.candidate_title: Limited anticipation of future capability needs
items.disposition: Narrow to a provisional Deployment question about anticipating gaps in evaluation coverage
items.recorded_source_correction: Treat domain-specific evaluation and HELM as evidence that evaluation coverage can be mapped for a specified use. Lead time and predictive value remain proposals. Keep the target separate from forecasts of model performance and the design of timely tests.

sources.title: Chen et al., Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation
sources.locator: 19 October 2026 version, §2e, printed pp. 27–28, and Appendix A.2, Table 4, p. 68
sources.establishes: The authors describe the shift toward evaluations of domain-specific workflows and the distinction between task completion and changes to whole workflows. They give related research directions.
sources.boundary: The discussion motivates measuring relevant workflows. It does not backtest forecasts of which abilities would require evaluation before a workflow emerges.

sources.title: Liang et al., Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
sources.locator: arXiv v2, abstract and main evaluation design
sources.establishes: HELM organizes scenarios and evaluation criteria and makes missing coverage visible within that taxonomy.
sources.boundary: An inventory can provide a baseline for detecting a future gap. The evaluation design does not measure a forecast’s precision or useful lead time.

sources.title: Handa et al., Which Economic Tasks are Performed with AI? Evidence from Millions of Claude Conversations
sources.locator: arXiv v1, abstract and data and method sections on occupational task mapping
sources.establishes: The study maps observed activity from one AI service onto an occupational task taxonomy. It gives a candidate input for monitoring changes in use.
sources.boundary: Platform-specific observed use is only one signal. The study does not establish which abilities are necessary to meet future workflow requirements or whether existing evaluations will miss them.

items.unverified_claim: It remains unverified in these sources whether information available at a given date identifies newly needed, insufficiently tested abilities before they become important in a real workflow, with lead time useful for planning.
items.proposed_title: Forecasting missing tests for emerging workflows
items.proposed_question: Which current evaluation results and field observations can anticipate abilities that emerging workflows will require and existing tests miss? Assess how accurately they identify those gaps and how much time they provide to plan evaluation.
items.evidence_check: Reconstruct time-stamped signals and the evaluation catalogue as they existed at each decision date. Compare forecasts with a simple continuation baseline and later, independently assessed workflow requirements.

items.candidate_title: Agreed priorities get lost in evaluation practice
items.disposition: Keep provisional as a Purpose question about implementing recorded priorities
items.recorded_source_correction: The earlier manuscript frames this concern. Its Section 4.7.2 is the editorial lineage for the question, while the public papers below provide evidence about reporting practices and existing remedies.

sources.title: Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting
sources.locator: arXiv v2, §4 on intended use, factors, metrics, and evaluation data
sources.establishes: The framework recommends documenting intended uses, reasons for metric and subgroup choices, and the corresponding evaluation evidence.
sources.boundary: The framework provides fields for making design choices visible. It does not establish whether teams implement documented stakeholder agreements.

sources.title: Ghosh et al., Evaluation Cards: An Interpretive Layer for AI Evaluation Reporting
sources.locator: arXiv v1, §§3.1 and 5, and Appendix B
sources.role: Additional reporting framework and empirical artifact audit
sources.establishes: The study combines public evaluation artifacts and applies structured reporting signals. The sampled records show missing information that affects interpretation and reproducibility.
sources.boundary: The authors distinguish artifact-side reporting from process-side commitments such as pre-run decisions. The corpus cannot tell whether an omitted detail was absent in practice or whether an agreed priority was lost.

items.unverified_claim: The inspected sources do not establish how often priorities that people actually agreed and recorded are omitted or altered between the evaluation plan, test design and public report, or which audits expose those departures reliably.
items.proposed_question: When stakeholders have recorded what an AI evaluation should address, can they trace each priority through the claims, measures and reports? Identify departures from the agreement and document why they occurred.
items.evidence_check: Follow one or more evaluations with a dated priority record. Have reviewers independently match commitments to planned tests, completed tests and reported evidence, then distinguish justified trade-offs, incomplete reporting and unaddressed priorities.

items.candidate_title: Accounting for delayed and indirect evaluation outcomes
items.disposition: Narrow to a provisional Purpose question about who and what the evaluation counts
items.recorded_source_correction: Chen et al. directly motivate considering different horizons in agenda setting. Schmidt Sciences’ item on preserving human agency is adjacent context and should be separated from direct evidence on how to set horizons or count non-user effects.

sources.title: Chen et al., Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation
sources.locator: 19 October 2026 version, §3i, sociology and anthropology paragraph, printed p. 44
sources.establishes: The authors ask how an evaluation agenda can give attention both to immediate harms and to longer-term risks.
sources.boundary: The passage motivates broader agenda coverage. It does not prescribe which outcomes or groups to include in an individual evaluation.

sources.title: Schmidt Sciences, The Science of Trustworthy AI: Research Agenda
sources.locator: §2.2, prioritized topic on preserving human agency
sources.establishes: The agenda proposes examining interventions that preserve human agency in collaboration with AI.
sources.boundary: The topic concerns one possible outcome. It supplies no basis for choosing a follow-up horizon, affected non-user population or resource boundary.

sources.title: NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.establishes: The framework asks organizations to identify and document impacts across groups and society and establish regular engagement to incorporate feedback about impacts.
sources.boundary: It is guidance for a process. Application-specific choices about which periods and effects to prioritize require further justification.

sources.title: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
sources.locator: Field experiment, discussion of limitations and footnote on short-term learning
sources.establishes: The field experiment separates performance during assisted practice from performance on a subsequent unaided exam. The paper finds that these outcomes can point in different directions.
sources.boundary: The authors describe their outcome as short-term. This study does not establish longer-run effects, effects on non-users or a general rule for evaluation boundaries.

items.unverified_claim: The reviewed material motivates considering affected non-users and later outcomes. It does not validate a process for selecting the scope under practical constraints or show whether credible alternative scopes would reverse decisions in a range of settings.
items.proposed_title: Choosing which delayed effects evaluations count
items.proposed_question: Which affected groups, shared resources and future periods should an AI evaluation represent for a specific decision? Document who sets the boundary and how credible alternatives change the outcomes considered.
items.evidence_check: For one decision, compare two justified outcome scopes and record how they change the decision. Treat estimation of delayed causal effects and validation of a chosen proxy as separate checks.

reproduce_packages.description: Pure Python 3.10+ stdlib replay of 801 literature records -> 438 formulations -> 327 active families -> 60 specific challenge seeds.

reproduce_packages.description: Exact integer branch-and-bound solver reproducing K=7..48 optimal sets, coverage comparison, and constrained editorial stress tests.
